feeds.https://afludiary.blogspot.com/feeds/pos: <item><guid isPermaLink="false">tag:blogger.com,1999:blog-21247748.post-7884587387687581972</guid><pubDate>Tue, 03 Nov 2026 11:10:46 +0000</pubDate>2026-11-03T06:10:46.842-05:00<title>Preprint: H5N5 virus transmission is driven by repeated cross-Atlantic introductions and transmission among high latitude seabirds</title><description><p>&nbsp;<a href="https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.10.29.762228v1.full.pdf"><img height="232" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiznZBk688Lga7BN-PJ2UdkKdHANgAp2ynI-Dvn-Mf2_vVU5qw6oM7fwCSo_QVRnsGMoklA3rW5xhlhGxqyBlWAQCJGxpn1BcW-pgEiFXXn-ZNIGBiFsF7k95miotPYlpgCxH6bnIwsYKB1rOGbitWztednzWhG3cM4aLaXSKHF18Qqbw4Sz8mv0Q/w465-h232/image.png" width="465" /></a><br /><br /></p><div class="separator" style="clear: both;">#19,399</div><p></p>While most of the world's avian flu attention is focused on&nbsp;<b>HPAI H5N1</b>, in <b><a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2024/11/norway-veterinary-institute-reports-1st.html">northern Europe</a>, <a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2025/01/more-reports-on-hpai-h5n5-in-iceland.html">Iceland</a>,</b> and parts of <a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2024/05/wahis-more-reports-of-hpai-h5n5.html"><b>Canada</b></a>, a different variant - <b>HPAI H5N5</b> - has been making substantial inroads in recent years, killing birds and spilling over into <b><a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2025/01/more-reports-on-hpai-h5n5-in-iceland.html">cats</a></b>, foxes, <a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2025/03/uk-aphis-more-detections-n13-of-hpai.html"><b>seals</b></a>, and <a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2024/05/wahis-more-reports-of-hpai-h5n5.html"><b>racoons</b></a>.&nbsp;&nbsp;<blockquote style="border: none; margin: 0 0 0 40px; padding: 0px;"><div><p style="text-align: left;">In 2024's <a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2024/07/cell-reports-multiple-transatlantic.html" style="font-feature-settings: normal; font-kerning: auto; font-language-override: normal; font-optical-sizing: auto; font-size-adjust: none; font-stretch: normal; font-variant-alternates: normal; font-variant-east-asian: normal; font-variant-emoji: normal; font-variant-numeric: normal; font-variant-position: normal; font-variation-settings: normal; line-height: normal;"><b>Cell Reports: Multiple Transatlantic Incursions of HPAI clade 2.3.4.4b A(H5N5) Virus into North America and Spillover to Mammals</b></a>, we saw evidence of multiple introductions of H5N5 into North America, most likely by <b>pelagic seabirds.</b></p></div></blockquote><div>While only rarely reported in U.S. birds (just <a href="https://www.aphis.usda.gov/livestock-poultry-disease/avian/avian-influenza/hpai-detections/wild-birds?page=1"><b>58 out of 20,539 USDA samples</b>)</a>, last November <b><a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2025/11/washington-state-doh-h5n5-avian.html">H5N5 infected and killed a resident of Washington</a><a href="#"> State</a></b> following contact with backyard birds.</div><div><div style="background-color: #ebedec; color: #363636; font-family: Arial, Tahoma, Helvetica, FreeSans, sans-serif; font-size: 16px;"><span style="font-weight: bold;"><a href="https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2211124724008088?dgcid=rss_sd_all" style="color: #3f3f7f; text-decoration: none;"></a></span><span style="font-weight: bold;"><div><span style="font-size: xx-small;"><br /></span></div></span></div></div><blockquote style="border: none; margin: 0 0 0 40px; padding: 0px;"><div style="text-align: left;"> Last March, in <b><a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/03/viral-creep-h5n5-update.html">Viral Creep: H5N5 Update</a>,</b> we looked at its evolution as it has spread across the United States;  shifting from almost exclusively<b> EA H5N5</b> prior to last fall, to largely <b>EA/AM H5N5 </b>since November 2025.</div></blockquote><div><div>&nbsp; <div style="background-color: #ebedec; color: #363636; font-family: Arial, Tahoma, Helvetica, FreeSans, sans-serif; font-size: 16px;"><div class="separator" style="clear: both; text-align: center;"><a href="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/a/AVvXsEj3qQuA5cjZ8zWNqSJ5XSZ5rgFHEwrCZwoxQLnGs-x_bmwL4qys7bsXOWwp2prLzf-Y_wPqjoRoVYGxNjs6ei1nfICHlaTOGZC9s1ba9PKP9EE4YY1Ih7Zwmlz1dignhSYE7VM-e0OCaMoMqh1I-a7o2A5-EWVgamuT-WghHRAROL7Yph0rHxsZnw" style="color: #007f7f; margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 1em;"><img alt="" data-original-height="400" data-original-width="764" height="258" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/a/AVvXsEj3qQuA5cjZ8zWNqSJ5XSZ5rgFHEwrCZwoxQLnGs-x_bmwL4qys7bsXOWwp2prLzf-Y_wPqjoRoVYGxNjs6ei1nfICHlaTOGZC9s1ba9PKP9EE4YY1Ih7Zwmlz1dignhSYE7VM-e0OCaMoMqh1I-a7o2A5-EWVgamuT-WghHRAROL7Yph0rHxsZnw=w492-h258" style="background: transparent; border-radius: 0px; border: 1px solid transparent; box-shadow: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.2) 0px 0px 0px; padding: 8px; position: relative;" width="492" /></a></div></div></div><div style="text-align: center;"><span style="font-size: x-small;">Based on USDA Data - Graph created with Gemini</span></div><div><div style="background-color: #ebedec; color: #363636; font-family: Arial, Tahoma, Helvetica, FreeSans, sans-serif;"><div style="text-align: center;"><br /></div></div><blockquote style="background-color: #ebedec; border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; color: #363636; margin: 0px 0px 0px 40px; padding: 0px;"><div><span style="font-family: inherit;">The USDA defines these two strains as:</span></div><blockquote style="font-family: Arial, Tahoma, Helvetica, FreeSans, sans-serif; font-size: 16px;"><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><b>EA </b>= Eurasian; <b>AM</b> = North American; the EA H5 (2.3.4.4) viruses are highly pathogenic to poultry.</span></blockquote></blockquote><blockquote style="background-color: #ebedec; border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; color: #363636; font-family: Arial, Tahoma, Helvetica, FreeSans, sans-serif; font-size: 16px; margin: 0px 0px 0px 40px; padding: 0px;"><blockquote><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><b>EA/AM:</b> reassortant of H5 goose/Guangdong and North American wild bird lineage</span></blockquote></blockquote>Over the past summer, once again we saw several reports (see <b><a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/05/norway-veterinary-institute-reports.html">here</a>,&nbsp;</b>&nbsp;<b><a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/07/preprint-hpai-h5n5-in-polar-bear-and.html">here</a> </b>and<b> <a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2025/08/svalbard-hpai-h5n5-detected-in-arctic.html">here</a></b>) of H5N5 in land mammals (<i>polar bears, foxes, walruses</i>) above the arctic circle.&nbsp;</div></div><blockquote style="border: none; margin: 0 0 0 40px; padding: 0px;"><div><div><p style="text-align: left;">Although its current threat to humans appears low (see <a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/07/preprint-lethal-human-h5n5-influenza.html" style="font-feature-settings: normal; font-kerning: auto; font-language-override: normal; font-optical-sizing: auto; font-size-adjust: none; font-stretch: normal; font-variant-alternates: normal; font-variant-east-asian: normal; font-variant-emoji: normal; font-variant-numeric: normal; font-variant-position: normal; font-variation-settings: normal; line-height: normal;"><b>Preprint: A lethal human H5N5 influenza virus isolate exhibits low pandemic risk traits</b></a>), there's still a lot we don't know about this emerging subtype.</p></div></div></blockquote><div><div>All of which brings us to a new preprint which builds upon earlier reports, and finds evidence that H5N5 is more mobile than previously thought. They also report that it is more commonly detected in <b>shore or seabirds</b>, than in ducks and geese, as is common with H5N1.</div><div><div class="separator" style="clear: both; text-align: center;"><a href="https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.10.29.762228v1.full.pdf" style="margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 1em;"><img alt="" data-original-height="281" data-original-width="622" height="203" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiX-_JSVdlyvUTn3Q-jny-cuBibEuq3MySQDhRI6_q-zDXKuSzeze_DpW5z_Eo5WoBB2igfs7o6TojLiVkF8yCqkVQs2sjJG_sOFJxsbGCIZNUvvujNOSkmmNPdYrZEmxsAbA4BYdpRrexOzp03MlTb9-U4dercmpIKEeADvWGyYEuPvebxqWMnjg/w449-h203/image.png" width="449" /></a></div><br />The authors suggest that its carriage by seabirds and shorebirds necessitates `<i><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><b>alternative surveillance</b></span>&nbsp;</i><b style="color: #2b00fe;"><i>strategies</i>',</b> and warns we may be missing cryptic transmission of the virus.</div><div><br /></div><div>I've only posted some brief excerpts. Follow the link to read the preprint in its entirety. I'll have a postscript after the break</div><div><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><br /><b><span style="font-size: large;"></span></b></span><blockquote><b><span style="color: #2b00fe; font-size: large;"><a href="https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.10.29.762228v1">H5N5 virus transmission is driven by repeated cross-Atlantic introductions and transmission among high latitude seabirds</a></span></b><div><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><br />Clara R Malekshahi, Nicole St. Clair Knobloch, Alvin Crespo Bellido, Alexa Simulynas,&nbsp; Stephanie Goya, Leigh Papalambros, William J. Fitzsimmons,&nbsp; Alexander L. Greninger, Adam S. Lauring, Jonathan Runstadler, Martha I. Nelson, Wendy Puryear, Louise H. Moncla</span></div><div><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><br />doi: https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.10.29.762228<br />This article is a preprint and has not been certified by peer review&nbsp;<br /><br /><a href="https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.10.29.762228v1.full.pdf+html"><b><span style="font-size: medium;"> Preview PDF</span></b></a><br /><br /><b><span style="font-size: medium;">Abstract</span></b><br /><br />In November 2025, the first global H5N5 infection was reported in a person in Washington State. Previously, these viruses had only been detected in seabirds and shorebirds near the Atlantic Ocean, suggesting potentially<b> distinct ecology from dominant H5N1 strains.</b></span></div></blockquote><blockquote><div><span style="color: #2b00fe;">Using 354 global H5N5 genomes, we show that H5N5 viruses have been carried by high latitude seabirds and shorebirds<b> across the Atlantic at least 9 times, with introductions more frequent in the fall and spring.&nbsp;</b>We reconstruct a plausible path of cross-continental movement via Arctic or sub-Arctic regions, followed by a year of cryptic circulation prior to human spillover.</span></div></blockquote><blockquote><div><span style="color: #2b00fe;">These data show that <b>H5N5 viruses have undergone far more intercontinental movements than previously recognized</b>, and exhibit host and geographic patterns that are fundamentally distinct from dominant H5N1 lineages. The distinct host ecology, geography, and movement, paired with the capacity to infect a person, suggest that enhanced surveillance may be warranted.</span></div></blockquote><p><span style="color: #2b00fe;">&nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp;<b>(SNIP)</b></span></p><p></p><blockquote><p><span style="color: #2b00fe;">Since its introduction into North America, surveillance and monitoring efforts for HPAI viruses are focused on H5N1 viruses in Anseriformes species. However, our data show that H5N5 viruses have been <b>repeatedly introduced and have persistently co-circulated alongside predominant H5N1 strains</b>, but with wholly distinct ecologies.&nbsp;</span></p><p><span style="color: #2b00fe;">These H5N5 viruses exhibit host distributions and geographic patterns of spread that are markedly different from those of H5N1,<b> necessitating alternative surveillance strategies</b> that are formulated to these lineages. </span></p></blockquote></div></div><blockquote style="border: none; margin: 0 0 0 40px; padding: 0px;"><div><div><p style="text-align: left;"><span style="color: #2b00fe;">The close link between H5N5 transmission and seabird and shorebird ecology suggests that these viruses may continue to move across continents and circulate cryptically in these species, while the human infection shows that these viruses could pose spillover risk.</span></p></div></div></blockquote><div><blockquote><p><span style="color: #2b00fe;">Increased surveillance in wild birds and mammals, as well as monitoring of key locations of repeated viral introductions, would be crucial for the prevention of further spread amongst wild birds and for the prevention of potential spillover into mammals.</span></p></blockquote><p><span style="color: #2b00fe;">&nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; <b>(<a href="https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.10.29.762228v1.full.pdf">Continue . . . )</a></b></span></p><p>Although this study is limited by small sample sizes, it does suggest that H5N5 may be better established in the environment than previously thought.&nbsp; Given its persistence in high latitude birds, and repeated spillovers into mammals, it is definitely worthy of our continued attention.</p><p></p><div></div></div></description><link>https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/11/preprint-h5n5-virus-transmission-is.html</link><author>noreply@blogger.com (Michael Coston)</author></item><item><guid isPermaLink="false">tag:blogger.com,1999:blog-21247748.post-5809322828425217965</guid><pubDate>Mon, 02 Nov 2026 19:24:27 +0000</pubDate>2026-11-02T14:24:27.431-05:00<title>Washington Adds 6 More H5N1 Infected Herds (n=40) -  Indiana Reports 1st Infected Herd</title><description><p>&nbsp;<a href="https://www.aphis.usda.gov/livestock-poultry-disease/avian/avian-influenza/hpai-detections/hpai-confirmed-cases-livestock"><img height="344" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgBkaGTRgdzp73mULoIor21-FXdEuyBADPLS3K19j6VV26FnnihpLNhEsq42Pz1-DNnm9Ic745B5pnuIfqU6qJ9k_STh2Mq9IX99FaIkTEFXUL0VzuTTsS4A_4NEYUzYN8cHd-9tpWRRKwyud8rkBOOsXll3VUerhU79uxw0X5OnuOOpGd6YL2naQ/w459-h344/image.png" width="459" /></a></p><p></p><p>#19,398</p><p>As the&nbsp;<a href="https://www.aphis.usda.gov/livestock-poultry-disease/avian/avian-influenza/hpai-detections/hpai-confirmed-cases-livestock"><b>USDA dashboard</b></a> indicates (<i>above</i>), 6 more dairy herds have been reported as being infected with H5N1 in Washington state, bringing to <b>40</b> the number identified since October 8th.&nbsp;&nbsp;</p><p>All but one have been reported from Yakima County.</p><p></p><div class="separator" style="clear: both; text-align: center;"><a href="https://www.yakimacounty.us/3226/Avian-Influenza-Bird-Flu" style="margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 1em;"><img alt="" data-original-height="669" data-original-width="763" height="350" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjIIWuB9ok8kmQdvIhZUgvR7owZzCsWnhpDrDjB-bS0LezlaToCoxiGUxcSRWP_P5-96seyIu1oUo60r9CW9Df911wj4a83hAA789a0rtiqmBne7sVpblOeddWtbNlvx_MF33ayUeptYQhsdiml9YxA9Mqor6K_O1Dqx-LODds5fW88Y7l6Rcqgyw/w400-h350/image.png" width="400" /></a></div><br />Although it is not yet reflected in the USDA dashboard, the USDA (h/t<b> <a href="@maggiemfox">Maggie Fox</a> </b>on <b>Twitter/X</b>) has posted the following statement on Indiana's first detection of HPAI H5N1 B3.13 in a dairy herd.&nbsp;<p></p><span style="font-size: large;"><a href="https://www.aphis.usda.gov/news/agency-announcements/usda-confirms-highly-pathogenic-avian-influenza-dairy-herd-indiana"></a></span><blockquote><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><span style="font-size: large;"><a href="https://www.aphis.usda.gov/news/agency-announcements/usda-confirms-highly-pathogenic-avian-influenza-dairy-herd-indiana"><b>USDA Confirms Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza in a Dairy Herd in Indiana</b></a></span><br /><br />Contact: <a href="mailto:APHISpress@usda.gov">aphispress@usda.gov</a><br /><br /><b>Milk Supply Safe; Considered Low Risk to Human Health and Safety</b><br /><br />WASHINGTON, D.C., November 2, 2026—Today, the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) National Veterinary Services Laboratories (NVSL) confirmed via PCR (polymerase chain reaction) detection of highly pathogenic avian influenza (<b>HPAI) H5N1 genotype B3.13 in a dairy cattle herd </b>in Indiana. This detection was a result of routine National Milk Testing Strategy testing, not pre-movement surveillance.<br /><br />This marks the <b>first reported case of HPAI in cattle in Indiana</b>. While dairy cattle in a total of 21 states have been infected since the start of the outbreak in March 2024, APHIS has seen<b> <a href="https://www.aphis.usda.gov/livestock-poultry-disease/avian/avian-influenza/hpai-detections/hpai-confirmed-cases-livestock">cases in previously unaffected states this year</a>.</b> APHIS is working closely with the Indiana State Board of Animal Health to conduct additional on-farm investigations, diagnostic testing, and epidemiological data collection to better understand the detection and prevent further disease spread.<br /><br />The detection does not change <b><a href="https://www.aphis.usda.gov/livestock-poultry-disease/avian/avian-influenza/hpai-livestock">USDA’s HPAI eradication strategy</a>.</b> Biosecurity is still key to mitigating the risk of disease introduction or spread between premises. APHIS recommends <a href="https://www.aphis.usda.gov/livestock-poultry-disease/avian/avian-influenza/hpai-detections/livestock/enhance-biosecurity"><b>enhanced biosecurity measures</b></a> for all dairy farms. Producers should immediately report any livestock with clinical signs, or any unusual sick or dead wildlife, to their state veterinarian.<br /><br />This detection does not pose a risk to consumer health or affect the safety of the commercial milk supply. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration is confident that pasteurization is effective at inactivating HPAI virus, and that the commercial, pasteurized milk supply is safe. Dairies are required to send only milk from healthy animals into processing for human consumption; milk from impacted animals is being diverted from the commercial milk tank or destroyed so that it does not enter the human food supply.<br /><br />According to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), HPAI viruses circulating in birds and U.S. dairy cattle pose a low risk to the general public in the United States. However, people who have job-related or recreational exposures to infected birds or mammals are at higher risk of infection and should take appropriate precautions outlined in <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/bird-flu/worker-safety/index.html"><b>CDC guidance</b></a></span></blockquote><p>To recap:</p><p></p><ul style="text-align: left;"><li>In addition to<b> <a href="https://agr.wa.gov/departments/animals-livestock-and-pets/avian-health/avian-influenza/hpai-(h5n1)-in-cattle-producer-resources">40 infected herds</a></b><a href="https://agr.wa.gov/departments/animals-livestock-and-pets/avian-health/avian-influenza/hpai-(h5n1)-in-cattle-producer-resources"> <b>in Washington</b></a>&nbsp;&nbsp;</li><li>There have been <a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/11/washington-hospitalized-avian-flu-case.html"><b>3 confirmed human infections</b></a>&nbsp;in Washington state (1 fatal)&nbsp;</li><li><a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/10/colorado-reports-1st-h5n1-in-dairy.html"><b>The first H5N1 infected herd reported by Colorado</b></a>&nbsp;in nearly 2 years</li><li>and now, this <b>first spillover in Indiana</b>.</li></ul><p></p><p>All in the space of 3 weeks.&nbsp;</p><p>&nbsp;</p><a href="https://www.cdc.gov/bird-flu/worker-safety/index.html"></a> are infected with avian influenza (AI) .<br /><br />   Carnivorous and omnivorous mammals such as raccoons , weasels , badgers , wildcats , otters , martens , seals , and finless porpoises<br /><br /> shared with relevant agencies , including the Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs and the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency, and special surveillance was carried out in areas to thoroughly clean and disinfect the interior and exterior of farms , facilities , and vehicles to preemptively block risk factors for the transmission of avian influenza .<br /><br />   Designation and operation of wild bird surveillance areas in accordance with the Avian Influenza Prevention and Control Guidelines<br /><br />  The Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency ( Chungcheong Region Disease Response Center ) and local governments, including South Chungcheong Province, have stated that they are continuing to monitor the health status of field response personnel, including those In addition , if suspected symptoms of highly pathogenic avian influenza (AI), such as the death of more poultry than usual, are confirmed , they must immediately report to the disease control authorities (1588-4060/9060) .<br /><br />Lee Chae-eun, Director General of Nature Conservation at the Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment, stated, “ As highly pathogenic avian influenza (AI) has been confirmed in wild mammals, specifically leopard catesses, again this year following last year, <b>we will strengthen surveillance and inspections to closely investigate whether there are any additional infections in wild animals</b> , and we will do our best to ensure the safety of field response personnel and the public . ” She added , “ We also ask the public to report any dead wild animals immediately without direct contact if they find them . ”<br /><br />  Lee Dong-sik , Director General of the Quarantine Policy Bureau at the Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs, stated, “ With highly pathogenic avian influenza (AI) confirmed in wild mammals ( leopard cats ) following wild birds, <b>the risk of outbreaks has significantly increased as the related virus has entered poultry farms</b>. ” He urged poultry farm officials to “ strictly adhere to basic quarantine rules , such as spraying rodenticides , ensuring the safe storage of carcasses, controlling the entry of outside people and vehicles, and disinfecting the inside and outside of the farm daily, to prevent wild animals from entering the farm . ”</span></div></blockquote><p><br />A little over 3 years ago, in<b> <a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2023/07/avian-flus-new-normal-when.html">Avian Flu's New Normal: When the Extraordinary Becomes Ordinary</a>,</b> I wrote about the numbing effect that comes with the constant barrage of HPAI H5 reports from around the world.</p><div><blockquote style="background-color: #ebedec; border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; margin: 0px 0px 0px 40px; padding: 0px;"><span style="color: #363636; font-family: inherit;">Events that were nearly unthinkable four or five years ago&nbsp;</span>(see&nbsp;<b><a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/06/preprint-mass-mortality-of-southern.html">Preprint: Mass mortality of southern elephant seals during multi-species outbreak of HPAI H5N1 on sub-Antarctic Heard Island</a>)</b>&nbsp;have now become `<i>the new normal'.</i></blockquote><p>While we may have become inured to these happenings, that doesn't make them any less impactful to our shared global ecosystem. What future challenges may arise from these continued viral insults to non-human species is difficult to predict.</p>But given our largely passive response to avian flu, we appear on track to find out.  </div></div></description><link>https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/11/south-korea-mafra-report-on-h5n1-in.html</link><author>noreply@blogger.com (Michael Coston)</author></item><item><guid isPermaLink="false">tag:blogger.com,1999:blog-21247748.post-6789993526158080807</guid><pubDate>Mon, 02 Nov 2026 09:26:38 +0000</pubDate>2026-11-02T04:26:38.622-05:00<title>Washington: Hospitalized Avian Flu Case Died - 3rd Case Reported</title><description><p>&nbsp;<a href="https://www.yakimacounty.us/2417/Media-Releases#docaccess-a54c817ca8cdbdcf2bec342f57bbdebb"><img height="181" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjM3vhhK_h8bKMnVeGLzUhPR7J8ZCg_yZgdWyFbHgmE2NGPuWG7PLhp8BJn0fANu0EojUxKzyV7rdM-v72xfOVwqTRQx4N1DLMJpFX2-QR_RsT09danN3TlmMrAtEH-Eq0tUj7oAKgskNMRZBYiWgi4Eu4K2TdDvKkYn2wGzTLNQPGkwX6v227JjA/w400-h181/image.png" width="400" /></a><br /><br /></p><p>#19,396</p><p><br /></p><p>While details are sparse, overnight the <a href="https://www.yakimacounty.us/2871/Health-District"><b>Yakima Health District</b></a>&nbsp;reported that their 2nd avian flu case of 2026 - <a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/11/washington-yakima-county-reports-2nd.html"><b>announced on Saturday</b></a>&nbsp;- has died, and that <b>a 3rd case</b>&nbsp;(<i>reportedly not severe</i>) has been identified.&nbsp;</p><blockquote style="border: none; padding: 0px;"><div><div><div style="text-align: left;">Today's announcement does state that <b>contact tracing</b> is being done on the newly reported third case, and contacts of the second case are being <b>monitored for symptoms</b>.&nbsp;</div></div></div></blockquote><div><div><br /></div><div>The Yakima press release follows, after which I'll have a postscript.</div><div><br /><blockquote><span style="color: #2b00fe;">For immediate release: November 1, 2026<br /><br />Contact: Stephanie Ruiz, Communications Specialist (509) 941-7364<br /><br /><b><span style="font-size: large;"><a href="https://www.yakimacounty.us/2417/Media-Releases#docaccess-a54c817ca8cdbdcf2bec342f57bbdebb">Yakima County Resident Dies from Complications of Avian&nbsp;Influenza</a></span></b><br /><br />Yakima, WA- The Yakima County resident who was hospitalized with severe illness after&nbsp;contracting avian influenza (bird flu) following <b>exposure at a dairy with infected cattle died</b> today.&nbsp;<br /><br />The Yakima Health District offers its heartfelt condolences to the individual’s family, friends, and&nbsp;loved ones during this difficult time.<br /><br />The individual had <b>underlying health conditions</b>. People at greater risk&nbsp;include dairy workers and others who have close or prolonged contact with infected animals or&nbsp;environments contaminated with the virus. Transmission of avian influenza between humans is&nbsp;extremely rare and has never been documented in the United States. Public health officials are&nbsp;continuing to monitor individuals who had close contact with the patient for symptoms.<br /><b><br /><span style="font-size: medium;">Third Confirmed Human Case of Avian Influenza</span></b><br /><br />The Yakima Health District is reporting a third confirmed human case of avian influenza in a&nbsp;Yakima County resident who was exposed to infected dairy cattle at a Yakima County dairy. The&nbsp; individual has not experienced severe illness or been hospitalized.<br /><br />The Yakima Health District is working with public health partners to<b> identify and contact&nbsp;individuals who may have been in close contact with the person to monitor for symptoms.&nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp;</b></span></blockquote><p><span style="color: #2b00fe;">&nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; <b>&nbsp;<a href="https://www.yakimacounty.us/2417/Media-Releases#docaccess-a54c817ca8cdbdcf2bec342f57bbdebb"> (Continue . . . . )</a></b></span></p><p>This press release goes on to state:&nbsp;</p></div></div><blockquote style="border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; margin: 0px 0px 0px 40px; padding: 0px; text-align: left;"><div><div><p><span style="color: #2b00fe;">To keep the public informed, Yakima Health District plans to update its avian influenza webpage every <b>Monday and Thursday at 2:00pm </b>with the latest available information, including confirmed human case counts in Yakima County. Updates will be shared as new information becomes available.</span></p></div></div></blockquote><blockquote style="border: none; margin: 0 0 0 40px; padding: 0px;"><div><p style="text-align: left;"><span style="color: #2b00fe;">For the latest information, visit <a href="http://www.YakimaHealthDistrict.org/BirdFlu"><b>www.YakimaHealthDistrict.org/BirdFlu</b></a>.</span></p></div></blockquote><p>The latest update (Nov 1st) shows:</p><p></p><div class="separator" style="clear: both; text-align: center;"><a href="https://www.yakimacounty.us/3226/Avian-Influenza-Bird-Flu" style="margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 1em;"><img alt="" data-original-height="512" data-original-width="501" height="400" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiYh2Iv9l0JLrX0OxdN8e3H9hjNQt_0mkRK2Hec62Yc1O3CId0HpXo8on8fBjXjeKqkjoIM4AhjBckffg_KOylX5QasWo3K74fYu4RBS1cx6UGHdaUdUsXHtrTtOkHqcITo78OlYTLgu5IC_3xi-zOz1z580twso4QdtSv0XkHeFGSl0QpZ5gMHQw/w392-h400/image.png" width="392" /></a></div><br />Hopefully local officials will be more forthcoming about the modes of exposure&nbsp; margin: 0 0 0 40px; padding: 0px;"><p style="text-align: left;"><b>Worth noting: </b>While `bovine' B3.13 H5N1 infection has generally been associated with<i> mild illness in humans</i>, this case is reportedly hospitalized with severe illness.&nbsp;&nbsp;</p></blockquote><p>This patient is described as having unspecified `<i>underlying health conditions'</i>, and of course, we don't as yet have official confirmation of the genotype (presumably<b> B3.13</b>).</p><p>First the press release, after which I'll have a bit more.</p><p></p><blockquote><p><span style="color: #2b00fe;">For immediate release: October 31, 2026</span></p><p><span style="color: #2b00fe;">Contact: Stephanie Ruiz, Communications Specialist (509) 941-7364</span></p><p><b><span style="color: #2b00fe; font-size: large;"><a href="https://www.yakimacounty.us/DocumentCenter/View/46817/103126_Second-Yakima-County-Resident-Tests-Positive-for-Avian-Influenza">Second Yakima County Resident Tests Positive for Avian Influenza</a></span></b></p><p><span style="color: #2b00fe;">Yakima, WA- The Yakima Health District (YHD), in coordination with the Washington State Department of Health (DOH), is reporting<b> a second human case</b> of avian influenza, also known as bird flu, in a Yakima County resident after <b>exposure at a dairy with infected cattle</b>.&nbsp;</span></p><p><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><b>The individual is</b> <b>currently hospitalized with severe illness and has underlying health conditions</b>.&nbsp;</span></p><p><span style="color: #2b00fe;">The risk of avian influenza infection to the general public remains low. People at greater risk include dairy workers and others who have close or prolonged contact with infected animals or environments contaminated with the virus. Transmission of avian influenza between humans is extremely rare and has never been documented in the United States.</span></p><p><span style="color: #2b00fe;">The Yakima Health District is working with public health partners to identify and contact individuals who may have been in close contact with the patient to monitor for symptoms. YHD is also continuing to work with impacted dairies and public health partners to identify people who may have been exposed to infected cattle, monitor their health, and provide guidance and resources to help protect exposed individuals. This includes providing testing for exposed individuals who develop symptoms to support prompt diagnosis and appropriate medical care.</span></p><p><b><span style="color: #2b00fe;">Symptoms and When to Seek Guidance</span></b></p><p><span style="color: #2b00fe;">Symptoms of avian influenza in people can include eye redness or irritation, fever or feeling feverish, cough, sore throat, runny or stuffy nose, muscle or body aches, headache, and fatigue.Illness can range from mild to severe.If you work on a dairy farm and develop symptoms after potential exposure to infected cattle, contact your healthcare provider and let them know about your exposure or the Yakima Health District at (509) 480-3770 for guidance.&nbsp;</span></p><p><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><b>Updated Information on Avian Influenza in Dairy Cattl</b>e</span></p><p><span style="color: #2b00fe;">As of <b>October 29, 33 dairy herds in Yakima County have tested positive for highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5N1.</b> The Washington State Department of Agriculture (WSDA)maintains updated information on confirmed dairy herd detections through its website. The Yakima Health District will also share public health updates and prevention guidance on its webpage: <a href="http://www.YakimaHealthDistrict.org/BirdFlu."><b>www.YakimaHealthDistrict.org/BirdFlu.</b></a></span></p></blockquote><b><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><a href="https://www.yakimacounty.us/DocumentCenter/View/46817/103126_Second-Yakima-County-Resident-Tests-Positive-for-Avian-Influenza">(Continue&nbsp; . . . )</a></span></b><div><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><b><br /></b></span>Those who work with poultry, wild birds, or dairy cattle are presumed to be at greatest risk of exposure to avian flu, but other exposures (<i>dogs, cats, other peridomestic animals</i>) are possible.&nbsp;&nbsp;<br /><blockquote style="border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; margin: 0px 0px 0px 40px; padding: 0px; text-align: left;"><p>There are also a handful of cases here in the United States where no known exposure was identified.&nbsp;</p></blockquote><p></p><div class="separator" style="clear: both; text-align: center;"><a href="https://www.cdc.gov/bird-flu/situation-summary/" style="margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 1em;"><img alt="" data-original-height="253" data-original-width="285" height="240" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgVdH48FYzF8ietmUkeXzVFD45zrh7sH-p5lLywJ5Uwwn04TRdjlnW5eYIAwe-aqOWiWnJn53LJQ3HeXQzyztr6Zptlgtlz3ohv-PZ9MoGwosBxBWndeybBwthl1ENSylnTjlP4wpkqS0p39ttZGX6C9KblB6J6LOqcuRqY_gAKiueXeIIALdjaCQ/s1600/image.png" width="270" /></a></div>&nbsp;<p></p><p>For people at the highest risk, the CDC continues to recommend the use of <b>PPEs</b> (see below).&nbsp;&nbsp;</p><p></p><div class="separator" style="clear: both; text-align: center;"><a href="https://www.cdc.gov/bird-flu/media/pdfs/2024/09/H5-Wear-personal-protective-equipment-09192024-FINAL-CLEAN.pdf" style="margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 1em;"><img alt="" data-original-height="831" data-original-width="626" height="494" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhHAQesVf3Br7wY2IKVwLDlvksYz5yCrUgpwVM-7RF5HCdcMV3ak-yKCgW6YQoVWEvbjX1pYN100j3SNApRtmanSiDmpe0NOl6NKD_Gtj6QbwjxB56DgU1sYTDw61McJxbhFSK35usKXmvuaeWwEeSS-0YjZnxJikCCrJW4Aogk3h8fzWvfMjubeA/w373-h494/image.png" width="373" /></a></div><br /><p></p> <p>In early October we looked at:&nbsp;</p><div style="text-align: center;"><a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/10/avma-how-can-veterinary-personnel.html"><b><span style="font-size: medium;">AVMA: How can veterinary personnel recognize and protect themselves from domestic cats infected with HPAI A(H5N1) viruses?</span></b></a></div><div style="text-align: center;"><br /></div> <div style="text-align: center;"><a href="https://avmajournals.avma.org/view/journals/javma/aop/javma.26.07.0582/javma.26.07.0582.xml"><img src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/a/AVvXsEiTkXfxnYqAjShYUrffAYIYrsiCcbwQM73HBYy7SEwSK_ilBZRPJuItRdquAupg4aPF6j7L4djEqhQ05nJdKcHpINcdx0ihsdIoHkCJTlcxU310mL86bho9UsD-zEsGXdj396oExPklySAV5NY5qpUlc6PuSayfmDqomwLImI4rZElpZ0c7ylZ1SA=w400-h285" /></a></div></div>And the CDC offers <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/bird-flu/risk-factors/bird-flu-in-pets.html"><b>the following advice</b></a> to pet owners on how they may keep their animals safe from avian flu, and what to do if they suspect infection.<div><br /><blockquote style="border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; margin: 0px 0px 0px 40px; padding: 0px; text-align: left;"><div style="text-align: left;">While the risk to the general public is still presumed to be low, it is not zero.&nbsp;&nbsp;</div></blockquote><p>Since every human infection is another opportunity for the virus to adapt, the steps we take today to reduce human exposure could conceivably lower future risks from the virus.&nbsp;</p><p>But for that to happen, people need to take the threat seriously.</p></div></description><link>https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/11/washington-yakima-county-reports-2nd.html</link><author>noreply@blogger.com (Michael Coston)</author></item><item><guid isPermaLink="false">tag:blogger.com,1999:blog-21247748.post-5393732815831027307</guid><pubDate>Sat, 31 Oct 2026 10:23:01 +0000</pubDate>2026-10-31T06:23:01.984-04:00<title>Colorado Reports 1st H5N1 In Dairy Samples Since 2024 - Washington State adds 4 more Infected Herds</title><description><p><a href="https://ag.colorado.gov/press-release/routine-milk-tank-testing-detects-colorados-first-dairy-hpai-case-since-2024"><img height="253" src="https://ag.colorado.gov/sites/g/files/lrnvjt4226/files/inline-images/HPAI%202026-2.png" width="450" /></a>&nbsp;<br /><br /></p><p>#19,394</p><p>Just 24 hours ago I reported that Washington State had added<b>&nbsp;<a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/10/washington-state-reports-3-more-dairy.html" style="font-feature-settings: normal; font-kerning: auto; font-language-override: normal; font-optical-sizing: auto; font-size-adjust: none; font-stretch: normal; font-variant-alternates: normal; font-variant-east-asian: normal; font-variant-emoji: normal; font-variant-numeric: normal; font-variant-position: normal; font-variation-settings: normal; line-height: normal;">3 More Dairy Herds Infected with H5N1 (n=30)</a>,</b> but yesterday the <a href="https://agr.wa.gov/departments/animals-livestock-and-pets/avian-health/avian-influenza/hpai-(h5n1)-in-cattle-producer-resources"><b>WSDA added 4 more herds</b></a> to their rapidly expanding list.&nbsp;</p><p></p><div class="separator" style="clear: both; text-align: center;"><a href="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgj6jQaXQgRmwRqWxG8FNt73GISEd6zbo1bk2krDtm0s-XfvMMnyWMBlLh_86dee35kDiqC4G3__lFCUlsCejavCDmVt4_vzgiuKOB5sndV9xX7k99JqDAION0GoOEIsoDq6QJ_tiMnLi9-iEfNQrTAE2Xul7YJ6h7CdeAKnHsC3jEvQauddgp5ug/s1600/image.png" style="margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 1em;"><img alt="" data-original-height="603" data-original-width="719" height="336" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgj6jQaXQgRmwRqWxG8FNt73GISEd6zbo1bk2krDtm0s-XfvMMnyWMBlLh_86dee35kDiqC4G3__lFCUlsCejavCDmVt4_vzgiuKOB5sndV9xX7k99JqDAION0GoOEIsoDq6QJ_tiMnLi9-iEfNQrTAE2Xul7YJ6h7CdeAKnHsC3jEvQauddgp5ug/w400-h336/image.png" width="400" /></a></div><br />Meanwhile, Colorado - which was one of the earliest affected states back in 2024 - is reporting its first detection in bulk milk in almost 2 years. The following press release was published yesterday by Colorado's Department of Agriculture.<div><br /></div><div><br /></div><blockquote style="border: none; margin: 0 0 0 40px; padding: 0px;"><div style="text-align: left;"><b><span style="color: #2b00fe; font-size: large;"><a href="https://ag.colorado.gov/press-release/routine-milk-tank-testing-detects-colorados-first-dairy-hpai-case-since-2024">Routine Milk Tank Testing Detects Colorado's First Dairy HPAI Case Since 2024</a></span></b></div></blockquote><div><blockquote><span style="color: #2b00fe;">Friday, October 30, 2026&nbsp;</span></blockquote><blockquote><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><b>The risk to the general public is low and pasteurized milk continues to be safe because pasteurization kills viruses </b><br /><br />The U.S. Department of Agriculture’s National Veterinary Services Laboratory (NVSL) has confirmed a detection of Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) in a dairy in Weld County. This is the first HPAI detection in a Colorado dairy since August 2024. Since the initial detection of HPAI in dairy cattle in April 2024, Colorado has implemented routine bulk milk tank surveillance testing to ensure Colorado’s milk supply is not impacted. <br /><br />“This detection underscores the importance of our routine bulk milk tank testing to keep our herds healthy and our food supply secure,” said Colorado State Veterinarian Dr. Maggie Baldwin. “Colorado has taken a proactive approach to monitoring and responding to avian influenza, ensuring that early detection leads to swift mitigation measures to protect consumers and our food supply.”<br /><br />The Colorado State Veterinarian’s Office was notified by the Colorado State University Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory that <b>a sample from a routine bulk milk tank test tested presumptive positive for HPAI. The National Veterinary Services Laboratory (NVSL) issued the official confirmation of the detection of HPAI (B3.13 strain) in a dairy in Weld county on Saturday, October 24. </b>The dairy has been put under a quarantine order. <br /><br />Under the quarantine order, several mandatory stipulations are in effect to prevent further transmission of the virus. The quarantine restricts the movement of lactating dairy cattle from the affected facility. In addition, the operation must immediately implement strict biosecurity protocols across all farm activities and daily routines. To monitor and verify disease status, weekly bulk milk tank testing is required until two consecutive negative test results are obtained at least one week apart.<br /><br />CDA is working closely with the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment and local partners to protect the health of farmworkers and facility staff. Public health officials routinely monitor individuals following potential exposure to infected animals or raw animal products as a standard precaution. People most at risk for avian flu are those who come directly into contact with infected birds or other animals. The risk to the general public remains low and pasteurized milk continues to be safe, because pasteurization kills viruses. <br /><br />Colorado originally confirmed its first positive detection of HPAI in dairy cattle on April 25, 2024, during an outbreak that grew to affect 64 individual dairies across the state. In response to the widespread outbreak, Colorado became the first state in the nation to institute mandatory bulk milk tank testing for all commercial dairies in Colorado. That comprehensive monitoring effort successfully cleared all affected herds, with all dairies released from quarantine by December 2024.</span></blockquote><div><br /></div><div>Colorado was rightfully applauded back in 2024 for their aggressive response to their initial outbreak (n=64 herds) (see&nbsp;<a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2024/07/colorado-orders-mandatory-statewide.html"><b>Colorado Orders Mandatory Statewide Weekly Bulk-Tank Testing for HPAI</b></a>), which was copied by many states.&nbsp;</div><div><br /></div></div><blockquote style="border: none; margin: 0 0 0 40px; padding: 0px;"><div><div style="text-align: left;">It will be of considerable interest to learn exactly how this new case came about, and whether this is a one-off event.&nbsp;</div></div></blockquote><p>In Washington state, the big questions are what is driving the spread of the virus, and how long it may have been going on before it was detected.&nbsp;&nbsp;</p><blockquote style="border: none; margin: 0 0 0 40px; padding: 0px;"><p style="text-align: left;">Until we have answers to those questions, it is impossible to know whether these events are unrelated occurrences or the start of a new trend.&nbsp;</p></blockquote><p>Stay tuned.&nbsp;</p><p>&nbsp;</p></description><link>https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/10/colorado-reports-1st-h5n1-in-dairy.html</link><author>noreply@blogger.com (Michael Coston)</author></item><item><guid isPermaLink="false">tag:blogger.com,1999:blog-21247748.post-5238147932091037291</guid><pubDate>Fri, 30 Oct 2026 10:46:38 +0000</pubDate>2026-10-30T06:46:38.913-04:00<title>Washington State Reports 3 More Dairy Herds Infected with H5N1 (n=30)</title><description><p>&nbsp;<a href="https://agr.wa.gov/departments/animals-livestock-and-pets/avian-health/avian-influenza/hpai-(h5n1)-in-cattle-producer-resources"><img height="279" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjoBmul8RRLvEz0egxU4YQJwgJQKH4E15ZoOZ64GFC4NK-tYZwc7uBdIkjXXhautt1yLF3k8CjUTdIspDk4FP6W-PB1CBtW5Gx91LTN9AlpAbjIXIH2sXYQiGw2If8fItsQ3nNTc-gQOAUEd3TPvnwGBCwoZ5aNs4CmHpCpFY8r-mBb43ATezCnFg/w400-h279/image.png" width="400" /></a><br /></p><p>#19,393</p><p>In just 3 weeks the State of Washington has gone from never reporting H5N1 in dairy cattle, to reporting <b>30 infected herds</b>. Twelve days ago they also reported <b><a href="https://agr.wa.gov/departments/animals-livestock-and-pets/avian-health/avian-influenza/hpai-(h5n1)-in-cattle-producer-resources">a (mildly) infected dairy worker</a></b> was recovering at home.&nbsp;</p><blockquote style="border: none; margin: 0 0 0 40px; padding: 0px;"><p style="text-align: left;">Thus far, we've no information on how the virus (identified as<b> B3.13</b>) is spreading from farm to farm.</p></blockquote><p>While Washington State is the current hotspot for reported H5N1 in dairy cattle, over the past month two other states - Texas and Kansas - have reported outbreaks.&nbsp;</p><p>&nbsp;<a href="https://www.aphis.usda.gov/livestock-poultry-disease/avian/avian-influenza/hpai-detections/hpai-confirmed-cases-livestock" style="margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 1em; text-align: center;"><img alt="" data-original-height="617" data-original-width="814" height="388" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjylQKuU97MHYdMl6YkuK1BjiXdp4Fc5hms39tqhacSSOatZqATKkMoeMfu4VEKY_daVoRufcsoQzdO90GXPqMGd6wYcllCxOo8ywwXhj_1TdCl53dwQ4WG1IgAQiF0I4wXFs1-3SB8ZWyLsz9Qr3OGDfO95K9XCXPhbJmSuZRKVQuhVEnBGfSqmA/w512-h388/image.png" width="512" /></a></p><p>As we discussed yesterday in<b> <a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/10/preprint-why-americans-choose-raw-milk.html">Preprint: Why Americans Choose Raw Milk: Evidence from a National Quantitative Survey</a></b>&nbsp;- while Washington State <a href="https://kingcounty.gov/en/dept/dph/health-safety/food-safety/consumer-resources/raw-milk"><b>warns against the consumption of raw milk</b></a>, it also allows its sale in grocery stores.&nbsp;</p><p>Hopefully people are paying attention, not only to these outbreaks, but to the labels on the milk and milk-products they buy and consume.&nbsp;</p><p><br /></p></description><link>https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/10/washington-state-reports-3-more-dairy.html</link><author>noreply@blogger.com +0000</pubDate>2026-10-30T06:22:16.074-04:00<title>Hawaii DOH Reports H5N1 Genotype D1.1 in Wastewater on  Kauaʻi  </title><description><img src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/a/AVvXsEgwpszR5oBZpIdAzUczXv-Wu92NNY1hMlydBR71KpoDxyPFAi9PlRI2kJnA9dJh098Bz1Qr-8XGH19pj3rXKJqS7wDcDo08BamRtEcQu0-oxRpYqW6pHmBDvp-surdPSUApcghzVWOzTg6Nt-mlMakb3h83lg_luqKf_F8FZqy6n0RV1Lv9jDFGPQ=w320-h213" /> <br /><span style="font-size: xx-small;"><b>Hawaii lies beneath the West Pacific Flyway</b></span><br /><br /><p>#19,392</p><p>In November of 2024 the state of Hawaii reported their first ever detections of <b>HPAI H5N1</b>, first in a<b> <a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2024/11/hawaii-dept-of-health-statement-on.html">wastewater sample</a></b> on Oahu, followed by<b> <a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2024/11/hawaii-dept-of-agriculture-2nd.html">two outbreaks in captive and/or wild birds</a></b> the following week.&nbsp;Subsequent detections were made in wastewater on the big island,&nbsp;<a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2024/12/hawaii-dept-of-health-h5-detected-in.html"><b>in Hilo</b></a> in December 2024, and <a href="https://health.hawaii.gov/news/newsroom/doh-closely-monitoring-detection-of-h5-avian-flu-in-kaua%ca%bbi-wastewater/"><b>at the Wastewater Treatment Plant on Kauaʻi</b></a> in January 2025.</p><blockquote style="border: none; margin: 0 0 0 40px; padding: 0px;"><div style="text-align: left;">Proving this all wasn't just a fluke, in the fall of 2025&nbsp;<a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2025/12/hawaii-state-agencies-respond-to-3rd.html"><b>we saw at least 3 more detections.</b></a>&nbsp; While concerning, none of these outbreaks involved the<b> B3.13 </b>`bovine' or<b> D1.1 </b>poultry/wild bird strains, which together had caused scores of human infections in the United Stats.&nbsp;</div></blockquote><div><br /></div><div>Today, however, we have the first detection of H5N1 genotype<b> D1.1</b>,<b> again from a wastewater plant</b>, this time on the island of&nbsp;Kauaʻi.&nbsp;This was an environmental sample from an unknown source, and does not establish an infectious virus, a human case, or community transmission. &nbsp;</div><div><br /></div><div>First the DOH statement, after which I'll have more.&nbsp;</div><blockquote><a href="https://health.hawaii.gov/news/newsroom/doh-reports-h5n1-avian-flu-detected-in-kaua%ca%bbi-county-wastewater-sample/"><b><span style="font-size: medium;">DOH REPORTS H5N1 AVIAN FLU DETECTED IN KAUAʻI COUNTY WASTEWATER SAMPLE</span></b></a></blockquote><blockquote><span style="color: #2b00fe;">Posted on Oct 29, 2026 in <a href="https://health.hawaii.gov/news/category/newsroom/">Newsroom</a><br /><br />HONOLULU — The Hawaiʻi State Department of Health (DOH) is reporting that a wastewater sample from Kauaʻi County tested positive for H5N1 avian influenza. T<b>he sample was collected at a site in East Kauaʻi on Oct. 14, 2026</b>. DOH was notified of the result on Oct. 26. This is the first detection of the H5N1 virus associated with this year’s seasonal bird migration and the <b>first detection of genotype D1.1 in Hawaiʻi.</b><br /><br />In the United States, genotype D1.1 has become the predominant genotype in infected wildlife and domestic poultry and there have also been isolated events of D1.1 infecting dairy cattle. DOH continues to test milk from the local dairy and there have been no detections of H5N1. A small number of human cases of genotype D1.1 have been reported nationally. Human cases of avian flu are rare, and most cases have not caused severe illness. No human-to-human transmission of H5N1 has been reported. <b>Genotype A3 was the strain previously detected in Hawaiʻi.</b><br /><br />“While the risk to the public remains low, avian influenza can cause severe illness and high mortality among certain bird populations, including poultry,” said Deputy State Epidemiologist, Dr. Nathan Tan..“Commercial poultry producers and residents with backyard flocks are strongly advised to <a href="https://hdoa.hawaii.gov/ai/ldc/adconcerns/aiinfo/biosec/">increase biosecurity measures</a> to reduce the risk of infection. Avian influenza can also infect dairy cows and while pasteurized milk is safe to consume, raw milk should be avoided.”<br /><br />For the municipal wastewater sample collected on Oct. 14 by Kauaʻi County, digital polymerase chain reaction (dPCR) testing did not detect H5 avian influenza. However, <b>genomic sequencing identified genetic material from H5N1 avian influenza genotype D1.1.</b> The difference in results is not unusual: dPCR tests for specific genetic targets, while sequencing can identify genetic material present in very small amounts. <b>A subsequent sample collected on Oct. 21 tested negative for H5 avian influenza by dPCR;</b> <u>genomic sequencing results for that sample are still being processed.</u><br /><br />It is important to note that the detection of H5 genetic material in wastewater does not mean that live, infectious virus is present. Wastewater testing also cannot determine whether the source of the genetic material is animal, human or environmental contamination. An H5 signal does not confirm a clinical case or indicate community transmission. Instead, it serves as an early indicator that can prompt increased awareness and monitoring. The East Kauaʻi wastewater treatment plant is an open system, meaning the detection could be associated with a variety of sources, including contaminated products or waste from infected animals or people.<br /><br />Wastewater sampling is routinely conducted across Hawaiʻi to support infectious disease surveillance. Samples are sent to the DOH State Laboratories Division (SLD) for dPCR testing, as well as to the University of Missouri for advanced genomic sequencing to identify bacterial and viral genetic material associated with community infections. Using both methods provides complementary information and strengthens Hawaiʻi’s ability to detect low-level signals in wastewater. In addition to SLD’s testing, H5 avian influenza is monitored in other Hawaiʻi counties through the National Wastewater Surveillance System (NWSS) and WastewaterSCAN.<br /><br />The Hawaiʻi Department of Agriculture and Biosecurity (HDAB) recommends the following precautions for residents who need to remove a dead wild bird from their property:</span></blockquote><blockquote><ul style="text-align: left;"><li><span style="color: #2b00fe;">Wear disposable gloves or turn a plastic bag inside out and use it to pick up the carcass.</span></li><li><span style="color: #2b00fe;">Double-bag the carcass and dispose of it with regular trash.</span></li><li><span style="color: #2b00fe;">Wash your hands and disinfect your clothing and shoes after handling a dead wild bird.</span></li><li><span style="color: #2b00fe;">Monitor for any health symptoms that may develop afterward.</span></li></ul><span style="color: #2b00fe;">To report multiple or unusual illnesses in poultry, livestock or other wild birds or animals on any island in the state, contact HDAB’s Animal Industry Division at 808-483-7100 or email <a href="mailto:hdoa.ldc@hawaii.gov">hdoa.ldc@hawaii.gov</a>, Monday through Friday, from 7:45 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. For reports outside business hours or on holidays, call 808-837-8092.<br /><br />Residents who believe they may have been exposed to sick birds or other wildlife should contact the DOH Disease Outbreak Control Division’s Disease Reporting Line at 808-586-4586 for additional guidance.</span></blockquote><p>Roughly 5 months after the first outbreak, Hawaii's DOH&nbsp;<a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2025/03/hawaii-doh-launches-bird-flu-survey-for.html" style="font-feature-settings: normal; font-kerning: auto; font-language-override: normal; font-optical-sizing: auto; font-size-adjust: none; font-stretch: normal; font-variant-alternates: normal; font-variant-east-asian: normal; font-variant-emoji: normal; font-variant-numeric: normal; font-variant-position: normal; font-variation-settings: normal; line-height: normal;"><b>Launched a Bird Flu Survey For Backyard Flock Owners &amp; Bird Rescuers</b></a>, whose <a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2025/07/hawaii-findings-from-doh-bird-flu.html"><b>findings were published over the summer of 2025.&nbsp;</b></a>&nbsp;</p><blockquote style="border: none; margin: 0 0 0 40px; padding: 0px;"><div style="background-color: #ebedec; text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: inherit;">The survey was restricted to local residents aged 18 years or older who either keep birds at home, perform animal rescue, or engage in other bird-related activities. </span></div></blockquote><div style="background-color: #ebedec;"><p style="color: #363636;"><span style="font-family: inherit;">As the following excerpt from the Hawaii DOH press release indicates, there were significant gaps in the understanding of bird flu risks, and best practices, among these high-risk cohorts.&nbsp;</span><br /><br /></p></div><blockquote style="background-color: #ebedec; border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; color: #363636; margin: 0px 0px 0px 40px; padding: 0px;"><div style="font-family: Arial, Tahoma, Helvetica, FreeSans, sans-serif; font-size: 16px;"><p><b><span style="color: #2b00fe; font-size: large;"><a href="https://health.hawaii.gov/news/newsroom/findings-from-doh-bird-flu-survey-for-backyard-flock-owners-and-bird-rescuers/" style="color: #3f3f7f; text-decoration: none;">FINDINGS FROM DOH BIRD FLU SURVEY FOR BACKYARD FLOCK OWNERS AND BIRD RESCUERS</a></span></b></p></div><div><p><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><span style="font-family: inherit;">Posted on Jul 24, 2025 in <a href="https://health.hawaii.gov/news/category/newsroom/" style="color: #3f3f7f; text-decoration: none;">Newsroom</a></span></span></p></div></blockquote><div style="background-color: #ebedec;"><p style="color: #363636;"></p><blockquote style="color: #363636;"><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><span style="font-family: inherit;">HONOLULU — A survey by the Hawaiʻi State Department of Health (DOH) finds that <b>while most local residents are aware that the bird flu had been detected in Hawai‘i</b>, roughly <b>two-thirds of flock owners had been unaware of related best practices.</b><br /><br />In March 2025, the Hawaiʻi State Department of Health (DOH) invited Hawaiʻi residents who keep backyard flocks or are involved in bird rescue to participate in a survey aimed at gathering important data on bird flu awareness and preparedness.<br /><br />The <b>anonymous, online survey </b>collected information on the understanding of bird flu, as well as the practices and needs of those who keep poultry or care for rescued birds.<br /><br />Among the findings:</span></span></blockquote><blockquote style="color: #363636;"><ul style="line-height: 1.4; list-style: disc; margin: 0.5em 0px; padding: 0px 2.5em;"><li style="border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; margin: 0px 0px 0.25em; padding: 0.25em 0px;"><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><span style="font-family: inherit;"><b>About two-thirds </b>of backyard flock owners across the state reported they <u><b>were not at all familiar</b></u> with the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s <a href="https://www.aphis.usda.gov/livestock-poultry-disease/avian/defend-the-flock" style="color: #3f3f7f; text-decoration: none;"><b>Defend the Flock</b></a> recommended practices to prevent bird flu.</span></span></li><li style="border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; margin: 0px 0px 0.25em; padding: 0.25em 0px;"><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><span style="font-family: inherit;"><b>Two-thirds</b> of survey respondents also reported not knowing how to properly and safely remove and dispose of dead birds.</span></span></li><li style="border-color: currentcolor; src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjZuEakT4OCUqsA0OyyqzhUzAs1aWtbCzvLJHwE8F_PBpPbPX6rSS38RDxxPWBg7LOnsOq_IsOQTErHBCxe3nIN0QIJ445Imnbd1xWrtpEJXiHLetnc6kvX-QXHq6RIKCYPOaXjpbj2TC-mtuMK45XG6w-9Ety6hSkzVlWk7OgbucsXZOYww-Gwww/w400-h303/image.png" width="400" /><br /><br /></p><p>#19,391</p><p><br />With reports of H5N1 infected dairy herds increasing again&nbsp;(see <a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/10/washington-state-h5n1-detections-in.html"><b>Washington State: H5N1 Detections in Cattle Triple (n=27) - 2nd County (Benton) Affected</b></a>), we are seeing an uptick in <a href="https://agr.wa.gov/about-wsda/news-and-media-relations/news-releases?article=47359"><b>warnings from health departments</b></a> about the dangers of consuming raw milk.&nbsp;</p><p>The <a href="https://kingcounty.gov/en/dept/dph"><b>King County, WA Dept. of Public Health</b></a> unambiguously warns:</p><b><span style="font-size: medium;"><a href="https://kingcounty.gov/en/dept/dph/health-safety/food-safety/consumer-resources/raw-milk"></a></span></b><blockquote><b><a href="https://kingcounty.gov/en/dept/dph/health-safety/food-safety/consumer-resources/raw-milk"><span style="font-size: large;">Raw (unpasteurized) milk and raw milk products</span></a></b><br /><br /><b>Consuming raw milk and raw milk products can pose health risks.<br /> Raw milk and A(H5N1) virus‎</b><br /><span style="color: #990000;"><br /><b>The CDC recommends against consuming raw milk contaminated with live A(H5N1) virus as a way to develop antibodies against <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/bird-flu/situation-summary">A(H5N1) virus</a> to protect against future disease. Consuming raw milk could make you sick.</b></span><br />&nbsp;<br /><b><span style="color: #2b00fe; font-size: medium;">Why is raw milk unsafe?</span></b><div><ul style="text-align: left;"><li><span style="color: #2b00fe;">Raw milk is milk from animals, typically cows and goats, which has not been pasteurized. Pasteurization is a process of heating raw milk to kill germs from the animal that are present in the raw milk.</span></li><li><span style="color: #2b00fe;">Some people believe that raw milk is more nutritious than pasteurized milk; however, the major nutrients in milk are not affected by pasteurization.</span></li><li><span style="color: #2b00fe;">Raw milk and raw milk products, such as cream, cheese and yogurt can be contaminated with harmful bacteria and cause serious infections.</span></li><li><span style="color: #2b00fe;">People with weakened immune systems, young children, the elderly, and pregnant women are at increased risk for severe infections from raw milk and milk products.</span><b><span style="color: #990000;"> It is especially important that young children, elderly persons, and persons with weakened immune systems consume only pasteurized milk and milk products.</span></b></li><li><span style="color: #2b00fe;">Read the label! In Washington state, it is legal to sell raw milk but raw milk products must be clearly labeled.</span></li></ul></div></blockquote><p>In the fall of 2024, we saw similar warnings after a number of household pets were infected with H5N1, some presumably from exposure to raw milk and/or raw pet food (see&nbsp;<b><a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2024/12/la-county-issues-another-raw-milk.html">LA County Issues Another Raw Milk Warning</a>).</b></p>Despite <b><a href="https://www.fda.gov/food/buy-store-serve-safe-food/dangers-raw-milk-unpasteurized-milk-can-pose-serious-health-risk">ample evidence of its dangers</a>,</b> most states allow its sale from farms or co-ops, and some states - like Washington - allow it to be sold in grocery stores alongside pasteurized milk.<br /><p></p><div class="separator" style="clear: both; text-align: center;"><a href="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhL6ycyr1dWChcD4DfzovWXvGEI4up0HY79DLvIHQ9Be6IxWUpKjTP_K7RpxuOrxQ4na8byoBZTy5mJwF0C93mPKCJild0_agsnarllMdXZ1e0EvaEjLT_fcRUlyEbJm6aBXyEnGovVBZULsSz1lAjsHdkHKuWnOn8z3UiZz_j2h-wQ-rA-xdfLqQ/s1600/image.png" style="margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 1em;"><img alt="" data-original-height="477" data-original-width="632" height="302" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhL6ycyr1dWChcD4DfzovWXvGEI4up0HY79DLvIHQ9Be6IxWUpKjTP_K7RpxuOrxQ4na8byoBZTy5mJwF0C93mPKCJild0_agsnarllMdXZ1e0EvaEjLT_fcRUlyEbJm6aBXyEnGovVBZULsSz1lAjsHdkHKuWnOn8z3UiZz_j2h-wQ-rA-xdfLqQ/w400-h302/image.png" width="400" /></a></div><b>&nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp;</b><span style="font-size: x-small;"> State Laws on sale of raw milk - Credit CDC</span><b><br /></b><p></p><p style="background-color: #ebedec;"><b><span style="color: #2b00fe;">A</span> <a href="https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0362028X22067059?via%3Dihub">2022 study published in the Journal of Food Protection</a></b> found that<span style="color: #363636; font-family: Arial, Tahoma, Helvetica, FreeSans, sans-serif;"><span style="font-size: 16px;">:</span></span></p><blockquote style="background-color: #ebedec;"><span style="color: #2b00fe;">Results show that <b>4.4% of U.S. adults</b> reported consuming raw milk at least once in the past year, with <b>1.6% reporting frequent consumption</b> of raw milk (once per month or more often) and <b>1.0% reporting consumption once per week or more often.</b></span></blockquote><p>Today we have a new preprint - published Oct 28th - which suggests Americans' consumption of raw milk may be even higher than previously reported.&nbsp;</p><blockquote style="border: none; margin: 0 0 0 40px; padding: 0px;"><p style="text-align: left;">It is based on a survey of&nbsp;<b>1,075 eligible US adults</b> through an online panel in February of 2025, and it reports&nbsp;roughly<b> 15% </b>of US adults consumed raw milk in the preceding six months.</p></blockquote><p>While it is possible that pro-raw-milk enthusiasts were more likely to respond to this survey, recruitment was done through Qualtrics Research Services - using demographic quotas - not an openly advertised public poll.&nbsp;</p><p>I've posted the abstract below, but those wishing a deeper dive will want to follow the link to read the preprint in its entirety.</p><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><b><span style="font-size: large;"><a href="https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.10.26.26366487v1"></a></span></b></span><blockquote><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><b><span style="font-size: large;"><a href="https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.10.26.26366487v1">Why Americans Choose Raw Milk: Evidence from a National Quantitative Survey</a></span></b><br />Sophia Ruser, Cristina Rojo, Katherine J Koebel,&nbsp; Calvin Slaughter,&nbsp; Ece Bulut,&nbsp; Renata Ivanek<br />doi: https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.10.26.26366487<br /><b><a href="https://www.medrxiv.org/about/FAQ#unrefereed">This article is a preprint and has not been certified by peer review</a>&nbsp;</b><br />&nbsp;<br /><a href="https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.10.26.26366487v1.full.pdf+html"><b><span style="font-size: medium;"> Preview PDF</span></b></a><br /><br /></span><div><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><b>Abstract</b><br /><br />Raw milk consumption is a controllable source of foodborne pathogen exposure in the United States (US), yet existing national estimates of raw milk consumption behaviors are outdated and do not capture emerging factors such as consumers' trusted information sources, sociopolitical influences, and at-home risk mitigation behaviors. </span></div></blockquote><blockquote><div><span style="color: #2b00fe;">We conducted a nationally representative cross-sectional survey of n=1078 US adults to estimate the prevalence of raw milk consumption and at-home thermal treatment practices and identify predictors of these behaviors. Multivariable logistic regression models were used to evaluate predictors of raw milk consumption and thermal treatment behavior using adjusted odds ratios (aORs). </span></div></blockquote><blockquote><div><span style="color: #2b00fe;">Among <b>1,075 eligible respondents, 15% consumed raw milk in the last six months, including 5% exclusively and 10% in addition to pasteurized milk.</b>&nbsp;</span></div></blockquote><blockquote><div><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><b> </b>In multivariable analysis,&nbsp;<b>raw milk consumption was independently associated with younger age, cohabitation with high-risk individuals for foodborne infections (including children less than or equal to five years of age, and elderly, pregnant or immunocompromised individuals) </b>who had consumed raw milk, and perceptions of raw milk taste and safety.&nbsp;</span></div></blockquote><blockquote><div><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><b>Adults aged greater than or equal to 55 years had lower odds of consumption than those aged 18-24 years</b> (aOR, 0.05; 95% CI, 0.02-0.15), while those living with a high-risk household member who consumed raw milk had higher odds of consumption (aOR, 4.39; 95% CI, 2.69-7.22). <b>Perceiving raw milk to have higher risk of causing illness was associated with lower odds of raw milk consumption</b> (aOR: 0.32, 95% CI: 0.17-0.62) compared to believing the risk to be equal across milk types, and <b>thermal treatment was reported by 38% of exclusive raw milk consumers (n=58) and 47% of consumers of both milk types (n=106). </b></span></div></blockquote><blockquote><div><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><b>Raw milk consumption in the US appears to be substantially more common than previously reported and shaped by factors such as taste, safety, and household raw milk consumption among high-risk individuals for foodborne infections.</b> The proportion of raw milk consumers already practicing at-home thermal treatment suggests a potential opportunity for risk mitigation.</span></div></blockquote><div><br />While all of this is self-reported and unverified information, it appears <i>that among the respondents to this poll</i> that&nbsp;<b>high-risk groups</b>&nbsp;(<b><span style="color: #990000;">young children, elderly persons, and persons with weakened immune systems)</span></b> are often cited as household consumers of raw milk.<br /><ul style="text-align: left;"><li><b>10.0%</b> reported a child aged five or younger who had consumed it.</li><li><b>9.1%</b> reported an adult aged 65 or older.</li><li><b>3.2%</b> reported an immunocompromised person.</li><li><b>2.1%</b> reported a pregnant person.</li></ul></div><div>One potential bright spot, however, is the reported practice of <b>heating or steaming</b> raw milk (<b>44%</b> reported doing so <b>&gt; 50%</b> of the time). Whether their heating temperatures and times were sufficient to kill pathogens is unknown.</div><div><br /></div><blockquote style="border: none; margin: 0 0 0 40px; padding: 0px;"><div style="text-align: left;">Since we've seen multiple instances where H5N1 contaminated raw milk has reached store shelves (see&nbsp;<b><a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2024/12/california-cdfa-announces-another.html">California: CDFA Announces Another Recall of H5 Contaminated Raw Milk</a>)</b>, the risks - while low - are genuine.&nbsp;</div></blockquote><p>But whether any of this will dissuade those currently inclined to consume raw milk - after decades of near universal public health advice to the contrary - remains to be seen.</p><div> <div></div></div></description><link>https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/10/preprint-why-americans-choose-raw-milk.html</link><author>noreply@blogger.com (Michael Coston)</author></item><item><guid isPermaLink="false">tag:blogger.com,1999:blog-21247748.post-4989828881679450972</guid><pubDate>Wed, 28 Oct 2026 10:04:20 +0000</pubDate>2026-10-28T06:04:20.515-04:00<title>WHO: Fatal H1N1v Infection In Brazil</title><description><p>&nbsp;<img src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjf1gnuZd56FHCob7VTww7WTfu3vpBJAfQ0JcJzzc-qDCJmnxa3mA-ZJWDAjUC64WICIKEJsLOhdBYJ7hgFNulTI8wUqxIgBUt5lhaikNchBIM8LZl2kWppG-kZZhE1ebp7-1X2yRba2NydJmSFbwYiOhOec0Nt5Is_R44pt6-3M8dPAF28kmCspw/s1600/image.png" /><br /></p><p>#19,390</p><p><span style="font-family: inherit;">Overnight the World Health Organization published its latest&nbsp;</span><b style="font-family: inherit;"><a href="https://www.who.int/publications/m/item/influenza-at-the-human-animal-interface-summary-and-assessment--7-october-2026">Influenza at the human-animal interface summary and assessment, 7 October 2026</a>,&nbsp;</b><span style="font-family: inherit;">which describes one</span><a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/09/cambodian-moh-announces-6th-human-h5n1.html" style="font-family: inherit;"> <b>previously reported&nbsp;</b>&nbsp;<b>H5N1 case</b></a><span style="font-family: inherit;">&nbsp;from Cambodia, </span><b style="font-family: inherit;">4 recent H9N2 cases&nbsp;</b><span style="font-family: inherit;">reported from Mainland China, and </span><b style="font-family: inherit;">one fatal H1N1v case from Brazil</b><span style="font-family: inherit;">.</span></p><blockquote style="border: none; margin: 0 0 0 40px; padding: 0px;"><p style="text-align: left;">The H1N1v case is unusual in that the adult female patient - who had (<i>unspecified</i>) pre-existing chronic conditions - died after a month-long hospitalization. <b>Of note:&nbsp;</b>&nbsp;Her <u>husband and three adult children</u> also reported flu-like symptoms - were treated for a `<i>viral infection'</i> - but were never tested.&nbsp;</p></blockquote>According to the timeline provided by this report, the hospitalized case was only identified as having a novel flu (<b>H1N1v</b>) a week after her death.&nbsp; As a result, epidemiological investigation wasn't begun until September 5th,  roughly 7 weeks after she (<i>and her family</i>) first fell ill.<div><br /></div><div>First, the WHO report, after which I'll return with more.</div><div><br /><span style="color: #2b00fe; font-size: medium;"><a href="https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/influenza/human-animal-interface-risk-assessments/influenza-at-the-human-animal-interface-summary-and-assessment--from-7-september-to-7-october-2026.pdf?sfvrsn=ffb871ef_3&amp;download=true"><b></b></a></span><blockquote><span style="color: #2b00fe; font-family: inherit; font-size: medium;"><a href="https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/influenza/human-animal-interface-risk-assessments/influenza-at-the-human-animal-interface-summary-and-assessment--from-7-september-to-7-october-2026.pdf?sfvrsn=ffb871ef_3&amp;download=true"><b>Swine influenza viruses in humans</b>&nbsp;</a></span><div><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><br /></span></div><div><b><span style="color: #2b00fe;">Influenza A(H1N1)v, Brazil</span></b><div><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><br /></span></div><div><span style="color: #2b00fe;">On 30 September 2026, Brazil notified PAHO/WHO of a laboratory-confirmed human infection with an influenza A(H1N1)v virus in an adult woman, with pre-existing chronic conditions, residing in the state of Santa Catarina. <b>She developed symptoms of influenza-like illness </b>on<b> 16 July 2026</b> and sought medical attention on 20 July.&nbsp;</span></div><div><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><br /></span></div><div><span style="color: #2b00fe;">Her husband and three adult children, who live in the same household,also experienced symptoms of an influenza-like illness; at that time, all were diagnosed, based solely on clinical examination, with a viral infection and received treatment.</span></div><div><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><br /></span></div><div><span style="color: #2b00fe;">&nbsp; The woman, however, did not recover. <b>On 27 July, the patient was hospitalized due to worsening respiratory symptom</b>s. She received treatment, including the antiviral oseltamivir, and required intensive care, including ventilatory support. Despite intensive care, <b>the patient passed away on 28 August.</b></span></div><div><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><br /></span></div><div><span style="color: #2b00fe;">A nasopharyngeal sample, collected on 29 July, tested positive for influenza A on 30 July and was subsequently subtyped as <b>influenza A(H1N1</b>) on 31 July. The sample was sent to the reference laboratory for respiratory viruses at the Oswaldo Cruz Institute (IOC/Fiocruz) in Rio de Janeiro for further characterization.<b> On 4 September, genomic analysis identified an influenza A(H1N1)v virus.</b></span></div><div><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><br /></span></div><div><span style="color: #2b00fe;">According to information gathered during an <b>epidemiological investigation conducted by municipal and state teams between 5 and 9 September</b>, the patient had<b> no history of travel or direct contact with swine</b>. However, a possible indirect exposure to swine was identified through a neighbour who raises these animals for personal consumption.</span></div><div><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><br /></span></div><div><span style="color: #2b00fe;">Since 2015, twelve cases of human infection with swine-origin virus variants, including this one, have been detected within Brazil’s respiratory virus surveillance workflow.</span></div><div></div></div></blockquote><div><div><br /></div></div></div><div><div>This chronology illustrates just how difficult it can be to detect a novel virus, even when the patient is hospitalized with severe influenza. A few recent examples include:</div><div><ul style="text-align: left;"><li><span style="font-family: inherit;"><span style="background-color: #ebedec; color: #363636;">In November of 2025, Washington State reported the first known human infection with avian <b>H5N5</b>; a diagnosis that was delayed - according to </span><a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/05/mmwr-fatal-human-case-of-hpai-ah5n5-in.html" style="background-color: #ebedec; color: #3f3f7f; text-decoration: none;"><b>an MMWR report</b></a><span style="background-color: #ebedec; color: #363636;"> - by&nbsp;&nbsp;</span><i style="background-color: #ebedec; color: #363636;"><b><span style="color: #2b00fe;">`early and repeated <u>negative influenza test results</u> from upper respiratory swab specimens'</span></b></i><span style="background-color: #ebedec; color: #363636;">.</span></span></li></ul><ul style="text-align: left;"><li><span style="font-family: inherit;"><span style="background-color: #ebedec; color: #363636;">In 2024, a Missouri patient was hospitalized with influenza A, and released, before being notified they had <b>H5N1</b> (see </span><a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2024/09/missouri-dhss-human-h5-bird-flu-case.html" style="background-color: #ebedec; color: #3f3f7f; text-decoration: none;"><b>Missouri DHSS: Human H5 bird flu case confirmed in Missouri</b></a><span style="background-color: #ebedec; color: #363636;">).&nbsp;</span></span></li></ul><ul style="text-align: left;"><li><span style="color: #363636; font-family: inherit;">Also in 2024,<b> </b><a href="https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2024-DON519"><b>Australia treated a child with recent travel from India for severe flu</b>,</a> which resulted in respiratory failure. The child fell ill (in India) in late February, was hospitalized in Melbourne in early March, and was released after &gt; 2 weeks. While respiratory samples were taken in early March, they weren't identified as&nbsp;<b>H5N1 positive</b>&nbsp;until mid-May.&nbsp;</span>&nbsp;</li></ul></div><p>Complicating matters, most people experiencing mild or moderate flu symptoms are unlikely to seek medical care, and even when they do, they are often treated for a `<i>viral illness</i>' and never tested.&nbsp;&nbsp;</p></div><blockquote style="border: none; margin: 0 0 0 40px; padding: 0px;"><div><p style="text-align: left;">We've seen past studies (see <b><a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2013/06/cid-journal-estimates-of-human.html">here</a></b>, <a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2013/06/lancet-clinical-severity-of-human-h7n9.html"><b>here</b></a>, and<a href="https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3166087/"> <b>here</b></a>) suggesting that as few as 1 in 100 cases are identified in the community.&nbsp;</p></div></blockquote><div>In early 2025, the CDC issued a <a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2025/01/cdc-han-accelerated-subtyping-of.html"><b>HAN: Accelerated Subtyping of Influenza A in Hospitalized Patients</b></a>, requesting that all hospitalized patients with suspected influenza be subtyped within 24 hours.&nbsp;</div><div><br /></div><blockquote style="border: none; margin: 0 0 0 40px; padding: 0px;"><div style="text-align: left;">More recently, we saw&nbsp;<a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/10/washington-state-updated-guidance-for.html" style="font-feature-settings: normal; font-kerning: auto; font-language-override: normal; font-optical-sizing: auto; font-size-adjust: none; font-stretch: normal; font-variant-alternates: normal; font-variant-east-asian: normal; font-variant-emoji: normal;
