font-variant-numeric: normal; font-variant-position: normal; font-variation-settings: normal; line-height: normal;"><b>Washington State: Updated guidance for novel influenza screening and influenza subtyping</b></a>, which emphasized the importance of identifying those with acute respiratory illness (ARI) and specific epidemiologic risk factors.</div></blockquote><div><p style="text-align: left;">The reality is, it takes a certain degree of luck to detect sporadic novel flu infections in the community. While better screening methods could improve detection rates, many mild and moderate infections will still likely fly beneath our radar.&nbsp;</p></div><blockquote style="border: none; margin: 0 0 0 40px; padding: 0px;"><div style="text-align: left;">A reminder than anything we say about the current threat from H5N1, swine flu variants, MERS-CoV, or any other pandemic threat must carry an implied asterisk.</div></blockquote><p>A disclaimer that says, ` <i><span style="color: #2b00fe;">* based on available, and likely incomplete, information. . .  '.</span></i></p></description><link>https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/10/who-fatal-h1n1v-infection-in-brazil.html</link><author>noreply@blogger.com (Michael Coston)</author></item><item><guid isPermaLink="false">tag:blogger.com,1999:blog-21247748.post-6970960807509955744</guid><pubDate>Tue, 27 Oct 2026 11:52:37 +0000</pubDate>2026-10-27T07:52:37.812-04:00<title>Washington State: H5N1 Detections in Cattle Triple (n=27) - 2nd County (Benton) Affected</title><description><p>&nbsp;<a href="https://agr.wa.gov/departments/animals-livestock-and-pets/avian-health/avian-influenza/hpai-(h5n1)-in-cattle-producer-resources"><img src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhYRpzjY-WfMVEWvUWdM5zk295O3vKtMcuKzWkprLq4YgQpOwB4bPP0EQtSROkgF_62xEldX34VtYJIApoQJ0B6G4Vikgtm_SsmIpESTo4FNE_ZA2c_6puf0HzUEHphZBewYB8uA0n-CxiSdiaS0dkPbnvVhoY5qVe3Wh0pbzzbMcV-YajgH5fa0g/w400-h266/image.png" /></a></p><br />#18,389<p></p><p>While it hasn't shown up yet on the<b> <a href="https://www.aphis.usda.gov/livestock-poultry-disease/avian/avian-influenza/hpai-detections/hpai-confirmed-cases-livestock">USDA's H5N1 in Livestock dashboard</a>,</b> the number of dairy herds in Washington State infected with HPAI has jumped from<a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/10/texas-washington-report-more-h5n1-in.html"><b> 9 late last week</b></a>, to <b>27</b>, with a second county (Benton) now reporting an infected herd.</p><blockquote style="border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; margin: 0px 0px 0px 40px; padding: 0px; text-align: left;">Less than 3 weeks ago (Oct 8th) the <a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/10/wsda-washington-confirms-first.html"><b>USDA/APHIS announced the first detection of H5N1 in dairy cattle in Washington State</b></a>, which was followed a week later by the first (reportedly mild) human H5N1 infection reported in the U.S. in 2026 (see <b><a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/10/washington-state-confirms-human-avian.html">Washington State Confirms Human Avian Flu Infection</a>)</b>.</blockquote><p>Other than the (<i>above</i>) update to the <b><a href="https://agr.wa.gov/departments/animals-livestock-and-pets/avian-health/avian-influenza/hpai-(h5n1)-in-cattle-producer-resources">Washington State Dept. Agriculture dashboard</a>,</b> I have found no other public announcement of this jump in detections.&nbsp;&nbsp;</p><p>Yesterday, the WSDA<i> did</i> publish a statement on the detection of H5N1 in a second county, which also states:<br /><b><span style="font-size: large;"><a href="https://agr.wa.gov/about-wsda/news-and-media-relations/news-releases?article=47441"></a></span></b></p><blockquote style="border: none; margin: 0 0 0 40px; padding: 0px;"><p style="text-align: left;"><b style="color: #2b00fe;">Media note: WSDA will issue a news release for each new county with confirmed HPAI in cattle. Subsequent detections in previously announced counties will be posted online.</b></p></blockquote><p>Excerpts from yesterday's announcement follow:</p><blockquote><p><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><b><span style="font-size: large;"><a href="https://agr.wa.gov/about-wsda/news-and-media-relations/news-releases?article=47441">WSDA confirms HPAI in dairy herd in Benton County</a></span></b><br /><br />OLYMPIA – Oct. 26, 2026 – Washington State Department of Agriculture (WSDA) has confirmed a detection of highly pathogenic avian influenza <b>(HPAI) H5N1 in a Benton County dairy herd</b>. The virus was detected by the Washington Animal Disease Diagnostic Laboratory (WADDL) through routine surveillance, and the finding was confirmed by the USDA National Veterinary Services Laboratories (NVSL).<br /><br />The dairy herd is under quarantine and has employed strict biosecurity measures. Veterinarians are working to treat sick cows. Pasteurized milk products remain safe for consumers, and milk supply shortages are not expected. WSDA urges dairy farmers statewide to report any clinical signs of illness to their veterinarian, including:</span></p><p></p><ul style="text-align: left;"><li><span style="color: #2b00fe;">Changes in milk appearance (thicker, often yellowish to brown)</span></li><li><span style="color: #2b00fe;">Decreased milk production</span></li><li><span style="color: #2b00fe;">Decline in feed intake</span></li><li><span style="color: #2b00fe;">Fever</span></li><li><span style="color: #2b00fe;">Respiratory symptoms</span></li><li><span style="color: #2b00fe;">Changes in manure</span></li><li><span style="color: #2b00fe;">Steep drop in rumination and rumen motility</span></li></ul><span style="color: #2b00fe;">If you notice any of these signs, isolate affected animals and contact your veterinarian and WSDA at 360-902-1878 or <a href="mailto:ahealth@agr.wa.gov">ahealth@agr.wa.gov</a>. Most cattle affected by HPAI recover with supportive care with full herd recovery typically taking 4-6 weeks.<br /><br />“Seeing the virus move to another county is disappointing but our dairy farmers are working hard to implement their biosecurity plans, share lessons learned and help each other get through this,” said Washington State Veterinarian Amber Itle, VMD, MS. "This isn’t new for the country, but it is new for Washington. I’ve been in awe of how hard our veterinarians and dairy farmers work together every day to keep their cows healthy, keep their workers safe and keep operating despite all the uncertainty this virus brings with it. This detection was through routine surveillance enabling us to detect the virus before cows got sick. We hope this will help us to implement measures on farm to prevent transmission within or between other dairy or poultry facilities.”<br /><br />HPAI can spread between dairy cattle through infected animals and contaminated milk, equipment, vehicles, clothing, footwear and other materials or people that move between farms. Wild birds can also carry HPAI, but they are not considered the primary source of spread of the virus that affects dairy herds.<br /><br />Poultry are also highly susceptible to HPAI. Other states have reported infections in commercial and backyard poultry flocks near dairy farms affected by H5N1. Poultry owners, including those who keep backyard flocks, should remain vigilant for signs of illness and practice strong biosecurity to help reduce the risk of infection.<br /><br /><b>(Continue . . .)</b></span>&nbsp;</blockquote><p><b><a href="https://agr.wa.gov/departments/business-and-marketing-support/farm-to-school-toolkit/wa-grown-food-recipe-kit/foodtoolkit/items/milk/milk/facts">According the WSDA</a>, </b>there are&nbsp;nearly<b> 400 dairy farms</b> in Washington State, which suggests that over the past 3 weeks<b>&nbsp;</b>roughly <b>7%</b> of their dairy herds have tested positive for H5N1.</p><div><blockquote style="background-color: #ebedec; border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; color: #363636; font-family: Arial, Tahoma, Helvetica, FreeSans, sans-serif; margin: 0px 0px 0px 40px; padding: 0px;"><span style="color: #2b00fe; font-family: inherit;"><a href="https://agr.wa.gov/about-wsda/news-and-media-relations/news-releases?article=47359" style="color: #3f3f7f; text-decoration: none;"><b><span style="font-size: medium;">Dairy product safety</span></b></a></span></blockquote><span style="background-color: #ebedec; color: #2b00fe; font-family: Arial, Tahoma, Helvetica, FreeSans, sans-serif; font-size: 16px;"><br /></span><blockquote style="background-color: #ebedec; border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; color: #363636; margin: 0px 0px 0px 40px; padding: 0px;"><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><span style="font-family: inherit;">Pasteurization inactivates viruses and bacteria in milk, including HPAI virus, helping ensure the safety of the dairy supply. Infected cows can shed the virus in their milk, making <b><a href="https://doh.wa.gov/you-and-your-family/food-safety/raw-milk" style="color: #3f3f7f; text-decoration: none;">raw milk</a> </b>and other raw dairy products <b>unsafe for consumption</b>. Avoid raw dairy product consumption, and do not allow your pets to consume raw milk or other dairy products, or raw foods such as raw meat.</span></span></blockquote><div><br /></div>While the State of Washington posted the above warning on October 8th, Washington allows <b><a href="https://app.leg.wa.gov/rcw/default.aspx?cite=15.36&amp;full=true">the sale of </a><a href="https://app.leg.wa.gov/rcw/default.aspx?cite=15.36&amp;full=true">raw milk</a></b> in grocery stores, natural food markets, food co-ops, and direct-to-consumer farm stores.<div>&nbsp;</div><div>Hopefully, the public is taking these risks seriously.</div><p>&nbsp;</p><p><b></b></p></div></description><link>https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/10/washington-state-h5n1-detections-in.html</link><author>noreply@blogger.com (Michael Coston)</author></item><item><guid isPermaLink="false">tag:blogger.com,1999:blog-21247748.post-3360410888839809999</guid><pubDate>Mon, 26 Oct 2026 09:56:36 +0000</pubDate>2026-10-26T05:56:36.608-04:00<title>The UK's `Be Ready' Preparedness Campaign</title><description><p>&nbsp;<a href="https://beready.campaign.gov.uk/"><img height="320" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEh8MX_C4yXuacnCRIN1MDa7h27SG71FXm-eiHQxRVjFNkUHww38icVUEvm201Hr13V2QhzN2bXR7KJF8xG8uPzJTI4MGbT7th_ZqUshCh7xF_JxNELYUX6RN0lwZi45kxWhp-Pwzrgg4I3uzeK882ckICc3IuaWKR3xOOTvKGviEW9Q0I6SOcHhRw/w199-h320/image.png" width="199" /></a><br /><br /></p><p>#19,387</p><p>While Avian Flu Diary is primarily an infectious disease blog, individual and community preparedness (<i>for all kinds of emergencies</i>) is its secondary focus. In&nbsp; its archives you'll find hundreds of preparedness articles <a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/search?q=%23NatlPrep&amp;max-results=20&amp;by-date=true"><b>(link)</b></a>.&nbsp;&nbsp;</p><blockquote style="border: none; margin: 0 0 0 40px; padding: 0px;"><p style="text-align: left;">While calls for individual preparedness are common in the United States (see <a href="https://www.ready.gov/stand-ready"><b>National Preparedness Month</b></a>), in Europe is is far less often discussed.&nbsp;</p></blockquote><p>Eighteen months ago, however, the  <a href="https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/qanda_25_857"><b>EU made headlines after calling for all households to prepare for a wide array of disasters</b> </a><i>(see excerpts below).</i></p><p style="background-color: #ebedec; color: #363636; font-family: Arial, Tahoma, Helvetica, FreeSans, sans-serif; font-size: 16px;"></p><blockquote style="background-color: #ebedec; border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; color: #363636; font-family: Arial, Tahoma, Helvetica, FreeSans, sans-serif; margin: 0px 0px 0px 40px; padding: 0px;"><p><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><span style="font-size: medium;"><b>What type of crises is the EU preparing for?</b>&nbsp;</span></span></p></blockquote><blockquote style="background-color: #ebedec; color: #363636; font-family: Arial, Tahoma, Helvetica, FreeSans, sans-serif; font-size: 16px;"><span style="color: #2b00fe;">The EU is preparing for a broad spectrum of risks and threats, encompassing both natural and human-induced disasters. This includes:</span></blockquote><blockquote style="background-color: #ebedec; color: #363636; font-family: Arial, Tahoma, Helvetica, FreeSans, sans-serif; font-size: 16px;"><ul style="line-height: 1.4; list-style: disc; margin: 0.5em 0px; padding: 0px 2.5em;"><li style="border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; margin: 0px 0px 0.25em; padding: 0.25em 0px;"><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><b>Natural disasters</b>: floods, wildfires, earthquakes, and extreme weather events exacerbated by climate change.</span></li><li style="border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; margin: 0px 0px 0.25em; padding: 0.25em 0px;"><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><b>Human-induced disasters</b>: industrial accidents, technological failures, and pandemics.</span></li><li style="border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; margin: 0px 0px 0.25em; padding: 0.25em 0px;"><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><b>Hybrid threats</b>: cyberattacks, disinformation campaigns and foreign information manipulation and interference (FIMI), and sabotage of critical infrastructure.</span></li><li style="border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; margin: 0px 0px 0.25em; padding: 0.25em 0px;"><span style="font-family: inherit;"><b style="color: #2b00fe;">Geopolitical crises</b><span style="color: #2b00fe;">: armed conflicts, including<b> </b></span><span style="color: #990000;"><b>the possibility of armed aggression against Member States.</b></span></span></li></ul></blockquote><p style="background-color: #ebedec; color: #363636; font-family: Arial, Tahoma, Helvetica, FreeSans, sans-serif; font-size: 16px;"><b><span style="color: #2b00fe;">&nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp;(SNIP)</span></b></p>Last December, we looked at the launch of&nbsp;&nbsp;<a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2025/12/denk-vooruit-netherlands-national.html"><b>Denk Vooruit: The Netherlands National Citizen Preparedness Drive</b></a>, on how to prepare for the first <b>72 hours</b> of an emergency (<i>e.g. extreme weather, cyberattacks, terrorist attack, even armed conflict, etc</i>.).<div><br /></div><blockquote style="border: none; margin: 0 0 0 40px; padding: 0px;"><div><div style="text-align: left;">Two months ago, in&nbsp;<a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/08/uk-national-risk-register-2026-urges.html" style="font-feature-settings: normal; font-kerning: auto; font-language-override: normal; font-optical-sizing: auto; font-size-adjust: none; font-stretch: normal; font-variant-alternates: normal; font-variant-east-asian: normal; font-variant-emoji: normal; font-variant-numeric: normal; font-variant-position: normal; font-variation-settings: normal; line-height: normal;"><b>UK National Risk Register 2026 - Urges Citizen Preparedness</b></a>, we looked at the UK government's sobering&nbsp;<a href="https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6a50d66b1228eb26a4cab76c/National_Risk_Register_2026.pdf"><b>223-page handbook</b></a> for dealing with wide variety of&nbsp; disaster scenarios.&nbsp;</div></div></blockquote><div><div><br /><div style="text-align: center;"><a href="https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6a50d66b1228eb26a4cab76c/National_Risk_Register_2026.pdf"><img src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/a/AVvXsEi9j3Jx_QifF4qjeev4SzPGAV-mf2hno7cznC5Gy5o76NgdERlCv7dPyLMkUohhIxStz3WscBjhg_CHC4SAVl9AkPT6c_gjFo4ssRj4PO7pP5UUKtu09m-2QrcDGPncrLXaDAVhgYAfpid5Nx0bIt65EilVBnSDNxO7KoNV-C3QRq-o-TcG_3I1QQ=w188-h200" /></a></div><div><br /></div> Late last week the UK quietly launched a new citizen preparedness campaign, which has gained a degree of internet notoriety over the weekend.&nbsp;&nbsp;</div></div><b><span style="font-size: large;"></span></b><blockquote><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><b><span style="font-size: large;"><a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/news/households-encouraged-to-take-small-simple-steps-to-stay-prepared-in-an-emergency">Households encouraged to take small, simple steps to stay prepared in an emergency</a></span></b><br /><br /><b>Households are being encouraged to take a few simple steps to stay prepared if everyday services are temporarily disrupted, under updated advice published today.</b></span><div><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><br />From:<a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/cabinet-office">Cabinet Office</a> and <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/people/dan-jarvis">The Rt Hon Dan Jarvis MBE MP</a></span></div><div><span style="color: #2b00fe;">Published:22 October 2026<br /><br /><img src="https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/5a37da9ded915d5a5f965f9c/s300_cabinet-office.jpg" /><br />Advice helps people feel better prepared for events such as severe weather, which can occasionally affect services like power, water, and the internet.<br /></span></div></blockquote><blockquote><div><span style="color: #2b00fe;">Campaign bolsters UK’s preparedness for emergencies, in line with European peers including France, Ireland and The Netherlands.<br />Simple steps include actions that are completely free, like signing up to the Priority Services Register, a service helping utility companies identify people most in need.<br /><br />Households are being encouraged to take a few simple steps to stay prepared if everyday services are temporarily disrupted, under updated advice published today.<br /><br />The <a href="https://beready.campaign.gov.uk/"><b>advice</b></a> is the <b>first stage of a three-year campaign </b>to help households across the UK feel better prepared for events such as severe weather, which can occasionally affect services including power, water, phones and the internet.<br /><br />The campaign focuses on straightforward things people can do in advance, including signing up to the Priority Services Register - a service that helps gas, water, and electricity companies identify customers that may need extra support in an emergency - and keep a small supply of non-perishable food and bottled water at home. <br /><br />With storms last winter and the wildfires this summer showing how severe weather events can cause disruption to our everyday lives and impact the services we rely on, from phone signal to water and the internet, launching the campaign brings the UK into line with European peers who all run similar campaigns already. <br /><br />The government has worked with other countries to learn from their experience and best practice. For example, the advice to be prepared for three days of disruption that is at the heart of the UK campaign is also used by France, Ireland and The Netherlands. <br /><br /> The government has also worked closely with local resilience forums across the UK to root the advice in what works for local communities.<br /><br /><b>Dan Jarvis MP, Security Minister, said:</b><br /><blockquote><i><b>Those who can follow this advice should follow this advice. By taking simple steps to be ready for everyday emergencies like severe storms, people can reduce pressure on emergency services, helping them prioritise people who need more support in an emergency. <br /><br />This is just the sort of community-focused campaign the UK needs to improve our resilience as a nation. It will bring us into line with European counterparts, where advice like this is a normal part of everyday life.</b></i></blockquote>The ‘<b>Be Ready’ campaign</b> will build gradually over time. More than five hundred organisations across the UK, from charities to businesses, have already signed-up to share messaging and campaign assets within their networks and communities. Government channels like GOV.UK and social media accounts will also amplify content.  <br /><br />Over the coming weeks and months, social media and radio advertising will help reach audiences who may be particularly at-risk in everyday emergencies: families with young children and older people. <br /><br />To ensure the updated advice is relevant and accessible to all, the ‘Be Ready’ campaign has been built in collaboration with charities and campaigners that work with groups that are often under-represented, including people with insecure housing and people who use foodbanks. <br /><br />Many of the simple steps are quick and cost-free, like signing up to the Priority Services Register, and other steps are designed to be as low-cost as possible. The intention is that, if households that can take these steps do, emergency services will be able to prioritise those most in-need if an emergency were to happen. <br /><br />The Government has published resilience advice for households since May 2024. While the ‘Be Ready’ campaign has seen the previous “Prepare” website updated with new messaging and branding, much of the advice has not changed and remains evergreen for households to follow. <br /><br /><b>Laura Scott, British Red Cross Director for UK Resilience, said:</b><br /></span><blockquote><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><i><b>We can’t control when emergencies happen, but we can all take some simple steps to be prepared, so that when they do, we are ready to help our friends, families and neighbours. <br /><br />We know from our work across the UK that local people know their communities best and want to play a part when a crisis happens. Having clear and trusted advice for people, especially those who may be more at-risk, could help reduce the impact of crises and even save lives.</b></i></span></blockquote></div></blockquote><p>You can visit the UK's&nbsp;<b><a href="https://beready.campaign.gov.uk/">Be Ready Campaign webpage</a></b> for more details.</p><div><div class="separator" style="clear: both; text-align: center;"><a href="https://beready.campaign.gov.uk/wp-content/uploads/sites/252/2026/10/Be-Ready-Checklist_English.pdf" style="margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 1em;"><img alt="" data-original-height="606" data-original-width="491" height="382" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhumsrI25b17xL9H3R5FzdudhtXyFHbbLSDDuKWiHKU4PqHR8_l12Z1bc3gm7UxTbsJccYcn5kkGdrFPqRgRO6kj8TAP9ph0QPJlPNdcc9KrXbWiE9Po_8ELZkwLhj9sTwcun17Cv64EUP7fbh7Xrovb7wH7lYSUTsGL0O9c0Wn6FfrE-BIxRlAqg/w309-h382/image.png" width="309" /></a></div><br />As we discussed a month ago in<b> <a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/09/npm26-making-preparedness-priority.html">#NPM26: Making Preparedness a Priority</a></b>, I consider 72 hours the bare minimum level of preparedness, and would strongly recommend striving for&nbsp;<b>7 to 14 days.&nbsp;</b></div><div><br /></div><blockquote style="border: none; margin: 0 0 0 40px; padding: 0px;"><div style="text-align: left;"><i>But it's a start</i>. And once you achieve it, it can be added to over time.&nbsp;</div></blockquote><div><br /></div><div>While no one can predict with any certainty what the next big regional or national emergency will be (<i>in the UK, or anywhere else in the world</i>),&nbsp; a modicum of general preparedness can go a long way towards making a bad situation a little less dire.&nbsp;</div><div><br /></div><div><span style="font-family: inherit;">So . . . if a disaster struck your area today, and the <b>power went out, stores closed their doors, and water stopped flowing from your kitchen tap</b> for the next<b> 7 to 14 days</b> . . . do you already have:</span><div style="background-color: #ebedec; color: #363636;"><ul style="line-height: 1.4; list-style: disc; margin: 0.5em 0px; padding: 0px 2.5em;"><li style="border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; margin: 0px 0px 0.25em; padding: 0.25em 0px;"><span style="color: #660000;"><span style="font-family: inherit;">A battery operated <b><a href="http://www.weather.gov/" style="color: #3f3f7f; text-decoration: none;">NWS</a> </b>Emergency Radio to find out what was going on, and to get vital instructions from emergency officials</span></span></li><li style="border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; margin: 0px 0px 0.25em; padding: 0.25em 0px;"><span style="color: #660000;"><span style="font-family: inherit;">A decent <b>first-aid kit,</b> so that you can treat injuries</span></span></li><li style="border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; margin: 0px 0px 0.25em; padding: 0.25em 0px;"><span style="color: #660000;"><span style="font-family: inherit;">Enough non-perishable <b>food and water</b> on hand to feed and hydrate your family (including pets) for the duration</span></span></li><li style="border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; margin: 0px 0px 0.25em; padding: 0.25em 0px;"><span style="color: #660000;"><span style="font-family: inherit;">A way to provide light when the grid is down.</span></span></li><li style="border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; margin: 0px 0px 0.25em; padding: 0.25em 0px;"><span style="color: #660000;"><span style="font-family: inherit;">A way to cook safely without electricity</span></span></li><li style="border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; margin: 0px 0px 0.25em; padding: 0.25em 0px;"><span style="color: #660000;"><span style="font-family: inherit;">A way to purify or filter water</span></span></li><li style="border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; margin: 0px 0px 0.25em; padding: 0.25em 0px;"><span style="color: #660000;"><span style="font-family: inherit;">A way to stay cool (fans) or warm when the power is out.</span></span></li><li style="border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; margin: 0px 0px 0.25em; padding: 0.25em 0px;"><span style="color: #660000;"><span style="font-family: inherit;">A small supply of cash to use in case credit/debit machines are not working</span></span></li><li style="border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; margin: 0px 0px 0.25em; padding: 0.25em 0px;"><span style="color: #660000;"><span style="font-family: inherit;">An emergency plan, including meeting places, emergency out-of-state contact numbers, a<a href="http://afludiary.blogspot.com/2010/07/in-emergency-who-has-your-back.html" style="color: #3f3f7f; text-decoration: none;"> <b>disaster buddy,</b></a> and in case you must evacuate, a<b> <a href="http://afludiary.blogspot.com/2012/07/inside-my-new-bug-out-bag.html" style="color: #3f3f7f; text-decoration: none;">bug-out bag</a></b></span></span></li><li style="border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; margin: 0px 0px 0.25em; padding: 0.25em 0px;"><span style="color: #660000;"><span style="font-family: inherit;">Spare supply of essential prescription medicines that you or your family may need</span></span></li><li style="border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; margin: 0px 0px 0.25em; padding: 0.25em 0px;"><span style="color: #660000;"><span style="font-family: inherit;">A way to entertain yourself, or your kids, during a prolonged blackout</span></span></li></ul><span style="font-family: inherit;">If your answer is `no’, then you're got some work to do.&nbsp;</span></div></div><div><br /></div></description><link>https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/10/the-uks-be-ready-preparedness-campaign.html</link><author>noreply@blogger.com (Michael Coston)</author></item><item><guid isPermaLink="false">tag:blogger.com,1999:blog-21247748.post-8931242823463431011</guid><pubDate>Sat, 24 Oct 2026 09:28:45 +0000</pubDate>2026-10-24T05:28:45.030-04:00<title>Texas & Washington Report More H5N1 in Dairy Cows & FluView Wk 41 Update</title><description><p></p><div class="separator" style="clear: both;"><a href="https://www.aphis.usda.gov/livestock-poultry-disease/avian/avian-influenza/hpai-detections/hpai-confirmed-cases-livestock"><div class="separator" style="clear: both;"><img height="307" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiFX5ALsNMTPVgzcV2gemHlSbsN3hueT8BKVM_JiOAjam1b6Zf0djAJ6AfA_Hnz93BFS13jMTVqZVArxrvoBAFt8XoHOrHq3Tv7YxO6JB44qCl4eqKrGYdiHNzJ-puceVZcRuPo_AJxhLg7EgWsIDDA_xSO6GFDx26YTCEuGCGTBBzMIIEkJceCEQ/w400-h307/image.png" width="400" /></div><br /></a></div><p></p><p>#19,385</p><p>Just over 2 weeks ago (Oct 8th)<b> <a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/10/wsda-washington-confirms-first.html">USDA/APHIS announced the first detection of H5N1 in dairy cattle in Washington State</a></b>, which was followed a week later by the first (<i>reportedly mild</i>) human H5N1 infection reported in the U.S. in 2026 (see <b><a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/10/washington-state-confirms-human-avian.html">Washington State Confirms Human Avian Flu Infection</a>)</b>.</p><blockquote style="border: none; margin: 0 0 0 40px; padding: 0px;"><p style="text-align: left;">Since then, we've seen the number of infected dairy herds in Washington state rise to <b>3</b>, then <b>8</b> - and as of yesterday - <b>9</b>.&nbsp;</p></blockquote><p>Meanwhile, the <a href="https://www.aphis.usda.gov/livestock-poultry-disease/avian/avian-influenza/hpai-detections/hpai-confirmed-cases-livestock"><b>USDA reports</b></a> that Texas has detected<b> four&nbsp;</b>infected herds in the past 30 days, and Kansas has reported <b>one</b>.&nbsp; While details on how the HPAI virus was introduced into Washington's dairy herds, how it is spreading, and the genotype have been scant, overnight <b><a href="https://gisaid.org/resources/gisaid-in-the-news/highly-pathogenic-avian-influenza-outbreak-in-the-united-states/">GISAID announced</a> </b>the Washington human case was <b>B3.13</b>.</p><blockquote style="border: none; margin: 0 0 0 40px; padding: 0px;"><p style="text-align: left;"><span style="color: #2b00fe;">Recently, genetic sequence data was released on GISAID from a case of captive<b> <a href="https://www.aphis.usda.gov/livestock-poultry-disease/avian/avian-influenza/hpai-detections/mammals?page=1">American mink</a></b> and cases of dairy cows from Idaho and Utah from the <b>B3.13 lineage (ggFlu genotype E.2)</b>. Some of these sequences <u>presented mutations associated with antigenic drift/escape and mild drug resistance.</u> </span></p></blockquote><blockquote style="border: none; margin: 0 0 0 40px; padding: 0px;"><p style="text-align: left;"><span style="color: #2b00fe;">On 12 October 2026, the <b>first case of a human H5N1 infection this year was detected in Washington State. The sequence (<a href="https://doi.org/10.55876/gis8.261023hs">EPI_ISL_205571770</a>) clusters with recent samples from Idaho and Utah</b>, carrying <u>the same mutation in the NA segment.</u></span></p></blockquote><p>Yesterday, the <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/fluview/surveillance/2026-week-41.html"><b>CDC's weekly FluView report</b></a> noted:<b><br /></b></p><blockquote style="border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; margin: 0px 0px 0px 40px; padding: 0px; text-align: left;"><p><b><span style="color: #2b00fe; font-size: medium;">Novel Influenza A Virus Infections</span></b></p><p><span style="color: #2b00fe;">One confirmed human infection with avian influenza A(H5N1) virus was reported to CDC this week. To date, human-to-human transmission of influenza A(H5) virus has not been identified in the United States.</span></p></blockquote><blockquote><span style="color: #2b00fe;">The case was reported by the Washington State Department of Health and occurred in a <b>worker aged ≥18 years at a commercial dairy cattle farm</b> where highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) A(H5N1) virus has been detected in cows. This individual developed <b>eye irritation and upper respiratory symptoms, </b>which they reported to the local health department. Specimens were collected from the individual and tested at the state public health laboratory using the CDC influenza A(H5) assay during the week ending October 17, 2026 (Week 41). Influenza A(H5) virus was confirmed by the state public health laboratory. Additional testing conducted by CDC determined this was an influenza A(H5N1) virus. This is the first influenza A(H5) case associated with a dairy worker in Washington.</span></blockquote><p>While influenza activity in the United States remains low, the FluView report indicates it is rising.&nbsp; Since seasonal influenza continues to evolve, this year's Northern Hemisphere vaccine contains 3 new components (H1N1, H3N2, Influenza B).</p><p>A little over a month ago, in&nbsp;<a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/09/preprint-near-real-time-data-on-human.html" style="font-feature-settings: normal; font-kerning: auto; font-language-override: normal; font-optical-sizing: auto; font-size-adjust: none; font-stretch: normal; font-variant-alternates: normal; font-variant-east-asian: normal; font-variant-emoji: normal; font-variant-numeric: normal; font-variant-position: normal; font-variation-settings: normal; line-height: normal;"><b>Preprint: Near real-time data on the human neutralizing antibody landscape to influenza virus in summer of 2026 shows antigenic advance of H3N2 subclade K region D mutants and H1N1 D.3.1.1 Sa mutants</b></a>, we looked at some of this ongoing evolution.&nbsp;</p><blockquote style="border: none; margin: 0 0 0 40px; padding: 0px;"><div style="text-align: left;">Among their findings, the authors identified 72 serum <b>samples in which an H1N1 D.3.1.1 virus carrying G155E was more than t</b><u><b>wofold less effectively neutralized</b> than a comparable virus without that mutation</u>. Those samples tended to come from teenagers and young adults (roughly 15–25 years old).</div></blockquote><p>While it isn't clear how much - <i>if any</i> - impact this will have on this year's flu vaccine effectiveness, this week's FluView carries the following caveat:<br /></p><ul style="text-align: left;"><li><span style="color: #2b00fe;">Since Week 21 (the week ending May 30, 2026), 8<b>1.5% of the influenza A viruses reported have been A(H1N1)pdm09 </b>and among these, the majority have been <b>D.3.1.1 HA subclade</b>.</span></li></ul><ul style="text-align: left;"><li><span style="color: #2b00fe;">The A(H1N1) viruses detected this season are still A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses, which emerged in 2009 and have caused seasonal epidemics globally since then. </span><b style="color: #2b00fe;">Influenza viruses are constantly changing,</b><span style="color: #2b00fe;"> usually requiring updates to influenza vaccine viruses each season. Historically, influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses have changed less often than A(H3N2) viruses. </span><span style="color: #990000;"><b><u>Recently circulating influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses (which are in an HA subclade called "D.3.1.1") are dividing into different groups showing different genetic changes.</u></b> </span><span style="color: #2b00fe;">It is too early to know what viruses may predominate or to say whether there might be implications on flu vaccine effectiveness this season.</span></li></ul>In addition to these antigenic changes, we are also following concurrent reports of creeping antiviral resistance in H1N1 (see <b><a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/09/eurosurveillance-emergence-and-spread.html">Eurosurveillance: Emergence and spread of NA-I223V and NA-S247N double-mutant A(H1N1)pdm09 influenza viruses with reduced oseltamivir susceptibility in the Netherlands and beyond, 2023 to 2026</a>).</b><p></p><blockquote style="border: none; margin: 0 0 0 40px; padding: 0px;"><p style="text-align: left;">Last week I reported that the<a href=" https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/10/fluview-week-40-antiviral-resistance.html"><b> CDC had announced 8 H1N1 viruses tested over the summer showed resistance markers</b></a>.&nbsp; <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/fluview/surveillance/2026-week-41.html"><b>This week's FluView </b></a>leaves that number unchanged.&nbsp;<b>&nbsp;</b></p></blockquote><p></p><div class="separator" style="clear: both; font-weight: bold; text-align: center;"><a href="https://www.cdc.gov/fluview/surveillance/2026-week-41.html" style="margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 1em;"><img alt="" data-original-height="745" data-original-width="602" height="400" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjYRwxqEXlhYk8e8BSrvSLLCHKPlbl2PT-jdjf2KH6EBjJGpHF73X-4YCIc28Q3YuFbej1Yll47ZvdWr488maw1-a1izFa4UJkxuV4dN48LKmhBd4fm5788y_paD-8PtOgxiEppQWUn3QR8mfICZUSgXVI5jRmdh9R4fGCpBa61CLi7eAFiE2Kfyw/w323-h400/image.png" width="323" /></a></div><p>Our last stop is the <b><a href="https://www.aphis.usda.gov/livestock-poultry-disease/avian/avian-influenza/hpai-detections/commercial-backyard-flocks">USDA's poultry HPAI dashboard</a>,</b> which shows an October&nbsp; uptick in both backyard and commercial outbreaks.&nbsp; Although commercial operations see the biggest losses in birds, backyard flocks are more often affected.&nbsp;</p><p></p><div class="separator" style="clear: both; text-align: center;"><a href="https://www.aphis.usda.gov/livestock-poultry-disease/avian/avian-influenza/hpai-detections/commercial-backyard-flocks" style="margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 1em;"><img alt="" data-original-height="688" data-original-width="849" height="361" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhW691F4Rk6FYySY195x0JynfxWWVz3UIuSAtUHHAAVo8sWdggXBPr89qODM7M-lF2pbDHChyphenhyphenbW7cT4g03ThZcX8t4BZLLD7xwGTfjEXWi7M-BQuH0UniFQW3AOroEmtfLJjxRryrOG0CPXmiqjWPQFar711Jh5aeOBTUH0G1t3np58FIbF_2vmaA/w446-h361/image.png" width="446" /></a></div><br />While most commercial poultry producers have a good deal of experience in dealing with outbreaks, <a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/05/mmwr-knowledge-attitudes-and-practices.html"><b>surveys indicate</b></a> that backyard producers are generally less well aware of the signs of avian flu, and may be less inclined to wear PPE.&nbsp;&nbsp;<p></p><p></p><div class="separator" style="clear: both; text-align: center;"><a href="https://doh.wa.gov/you-and-your-family/illness-and-disease-z/bird-flu" style="margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 1em;"><img alt="" data-original-height="327" data-original-width="400" height="261" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiLtYYWRzJgiUbOVxAk6HOhyHjZ_h99dGvlHLmett1PGL2bYRFll4GMUNMlKtKzQwhGRUpNJkcjD5tTjxD3P40AqY5P8E-IjiqOukh9ZWeMgmtWvNDjYydR6ZyEMt_yzFg4mc6hlql5ps6z_8y7mTDzauJX0HJGJO8mN0BMF3-32FxycZGpGrOROQ/w320-h261/image.png" width="320" /></a></div><p></p><div>Attempts to convince high-risk poultry and dairy workers to get the seasonal flu shot - which is hoped will&nbsp;<a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2024/09/preprint-intelligent-prediction.html"><b>reduce the risks of coinfection and potential reassortment</b></a> - continue to yield <a href="https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12008562/"><b>disappointing results</b></a>.&nbsp;&nbsp;</div><p></p><p style="background-color: #ebedec; color: #363636; font-family: Arial, Tahoma, Helvetica, FreeSans, sans-serif; font-size: 16px; text-align: center;"><a href="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/a/AVvXsEgd--a594tF8G_LYPS-OJdG2VndQSLEZTla707F8iKmux9tJK6wlGj0dz0AqAc97QOQ3MRnjiBrdCTsOLlMF10W1wdPNvlEtMKUNRSS9e95qcuQsLwCdPtqxyYNFyJ74Iyz4qPQBXNl7Uwy3GBR1OVa2YeO_EYoonp9JmOKAk4h7rE1y0bJnl7-oQ" style="color: #3f3f7f; text-decoration: none;"><img height="266" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/a/AVvXsEgd--a594tF8G_LYPS-OJdG2VndQSLEZTla707F8iKmux9tJK6wlGj0dz0AqAc97QOQ3MRnjiBrdCTsOLlMF10W1wdPNvlEtMKUNRSS9e95qcuQsLwCdPtqxyYNFyJ74Iyz4qPQBXNl7Uwy3GBR1OVa2YeO_EYoonp9JmOKAk4h7rE1y0bJnl7-oQ=w236-h266" style="background: transparent; border-radius: 0px; border: 1px solid transparent; box-shadow: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.2) 0px 0px 0px; padding: 8px; position: relative;" width="236" /></a></p><div><span style="background-color: #ebedec; color: #363636; font-family: Arial, Tahoma, Helvetica, FreeSans, sans-serif; font-size: 16px;"></span><div style="background-color: #ebedec; color: #363636; font-family: Arial, Tahoma, Helvetica, FreeSans, sans-serif; font-size: 16px; text-align: center;"><span style="font-family: inherit;"><i>Antigenic `</i><b><i>Shift'</i> </b>or Reassortment&nbsp;</span></div></div><div style="background-color: #ebedec; color: #363636; font-family: Arial, Tahoma, Helvetica, FreeSans, sans-serif; font-size: 16px; text-align: center;"><span style="font-family: inherit;"><br /></span></div>While the severity and impact of this year's flu season remains unknown, we are seeing mounting pressures from both seasonal and novel flu which could potentially complicate matters. <div><br /></div><blockquote style="border: none; margin: 0 0 0 40px; padding: 0px;"><div style="text-align: left;">All reasons why I've updated my Flu, COVID, and Pneumovax vaccines, and will happily don an N95 mask in crowded indoor venues.&nbsp;</div></blockquote><p>None of which guarantees I'll come away unscathed this winter, but it certainly increases my chances.&nbsp; And at my age, I'll take any advantage I can get.&nbsp;</p></description><link>https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/10/texas-washington-report-more-h5n1-in.html</link><author>noreply@blogger.com (Michael Coston)</author></item><item><guid isPermaLink="false">tag:blogger.com,1999:blog-21247748.post-626104180495572633</guid><pubDate>Fri, 23 Oct 2026 09:23:35 +0000</pubDate>2026-10-23T05:23:35.977-04:00<title>Virological (Referral): Preliminary report on H5N1 highly pathogenic avian influenza in Utah mink, August 2026</title><description><p><img src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEir4YoEvWPBWlzocVUzk09YrX9NFJdlabZFFYvpIEmpTPpFUNnfvUgdpx0dHXCGB2XVy6LlOGpNzZd20Sy5YlFR68d3I6pi-U_6ShUtuKawBdVgjwx5Mkt2kAPqr1JWAtRzaCXlwSNrDx1_uHdpdpjxXG7YYYJhj9vdax41djgqHsx9IPXNMgzuxg/s1600/image.png" /></p><p>#19,384</p> Two months ago, in&nbsp;<a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/08/that-touch-of-mink-flu-h5n1-in-utah.html"><b>That Touch of Mink Flu (H5N1 in Utah Edition)</b></a>, we looked at a cryptic announcement of an outbreak of HPAI H5N1 at a mink farm in Utah.&nbsp;&nbsp;Mink - along with other members of the <i>Mustelidae</i> family of carnivorous mammals (e.g.<i> otters, badgers, weasels, martens, and ferrets</i>) are highly susceptible to both COVID and flu infection. <br /><span style="font-family: inherit;"><br /><span style="background-color: #ebedec; color: #363636;">Over the past 20 years we've looked at a number of concerning spillovers, including:</span></span><div style="background-color: #ebedec;"><ul style="line-height: 1.4; list-style: disc; margin: 0.5em 0px; padding: 0px 2.5em;"><li style="border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; margin: 0px 0px 0.25em; padding: 0.25em 0px;"><span style="font-family: inherit;"><span style="color: #363636;">2009's&nbsp;</span></span><a href="http://afludiary.blogspot.com/2009/10/that-touch-of-mink-flu.html"><b>That Touch Of Mink Flu</b></a><span style="font-family: inherit;"><a href="http://afludiary.blogspot.com/2009/10/that-touch-of-mink-flu.html" style="color: #3f3f7f; text-decoration: none;">,</a><span style="color: #363636;"> where at least </span><b style="color: #363636;">11 mink farms</b><span style="color: #363636;"> in the Holstebro municipality of Denmark were reported to be infected with a </span><b style="color: #363636;">variant of the human H3N2 virus.</b></span></li></ul><ul style="line-height: 1.4; list-style: disc; margin: 0.5em 0px; padding: 0px 2.5em; text-align: left;"><li style="border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; margin: 0px 0px 0.25em; padding: 0.25em 0px;"><span style="font-family: inherit;"><span style="color: #363636;">In 2007, an antigenically distinct </span><b style="color: #363636;">H3N2 Swine Influenza</b><span style="color: #363636;"> was detected in Canadian Mink, reported in a 2009 Journal of Clinical Microbiology study called&nbsp;</span></span><b><a href="http://www.labmeeting.com/paper/28758903/gagnon-2009-characterization-of-a-canadian-mink-h3n2-influenza-a-virus-isolate-genetically-related-to-triple-reassortant-swine-influenza-virus">Characterization of a Canadian Mink H3N2 Influenza A Virus Isolate Genetically Related to Triple Reassortant Swine Influenza Virus</a><span style="font-family: inherit;"><a href="http://www.labmeeting.com/paper/28758903/gagnon-2009-characterization-of-a-canadian-mink-h3n2-influenza-a-virus-isolate-genetically-related-to-triple-reassortant-swine-influenza-virus" style="color: #3f3f7f; text-decoration: none;">.</a></span></b></li><li><span style="font-family: inherit;"><span style="color: #363636;"><span style="background-color: #ebedec;">We've seen literally dozens of reports of spillovers into mink since, including the generation of </span></span></span><a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2020/12/who-2nd-update-sars-cov-2-mink.html"><b>mink-variant COVID strains</b></a><span style="font-family: inherit;"><b> </b><span style="color: #363636;"><span style="background-color: #ebedec;">which - </span></span><i style="background-color: #ebedec; color: #363636;">at least temporarily</i><span style="color: #363636;"><span style="background-color: #ebedec;"> - <u><b>circulated in humans</b></u> in Europe back in 2020 (see</span></span></span> <a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2024/02/preprint-emergence-spread-of-sars-cov-2.html"><b>Preprint: Emergence &amp; Spread of SARS-CoV-2 Variants from Farmed Mink to Humans and Back - Denmark, June-November 2020</b></a><span style="font-family: inherit;"><b><span style="color: #363636;"><span style="background-color: #ebedec;">).&nbsp;</span></span></b><span style="color: #363636;"><span style="background-color: #ebedec;">&nbsp;</span></span></span></li><li><span style="color: #363636; font-family: inherit;">Fresh alarms were raised in the fall of 2022 when <b>H5N1</b> began spreading rapidly through a large mink farm in Spain (see<b>&nbsp;</b></span><b><a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2023/01/eurosurveillance-hpai-ah5n1-virus.html">Eurosurveillance: HPAI A(H5N1) Virus Infection in Farmed </a><a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2023/01/eurosurveillance-hpai-ah5n1-virus.html">Minks, </a></b><span style="font-family: inherit;"><b><a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2023/01/eurosurveillance-hpai-ah5n1-virus.html">Spain, October 2022</a>)</b>.</span></li></ul><ul style="line-height: 1.4; list-style: disc; margin: 0.5em 0px; padding: 0px 2.5em; text-align: left;"><li><span style="font-family: inherit;">In 2023 we saw<a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2023/08/finland-thl-statement-on-avian-flu-in.html"> <b>scores of fur farms (both mink &amp; fox) in Finland hit by HPAI</b></a><b>,</b> resulting in massive culls.</span>&nbsp;</li></ul></div><div><p>Roughly a month later, in&nbsp;<a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/09/h5n1-in-utah-mink-updated.html" style="font-feature-settings: normal; font-kerning: auto; font-language-override: normal; font-optical-sizing: auto; font-size-adjust: none; font-stretch: normal; font-variant-alternates: normal; font-variant-east-asian: normal; font-variant-emoji: normal; font-variant-numeric: normal; font-variant-position: normal; font-variation-settings: normal; line-height: normal;"><b>H5N1 in Utah Mink (Updated)</b></a>, we looked at local reporting on the incident, but details on the actual outbreak remained scant.&nbsp;</p></div><blockquote style="border: none; margin: 0 0 0 40px; padding: 0px;"><div style="text-align: left;">Yesterday, we saw <span style="color: #2b00fe;"><a href="https://virological.org/t/preliminary-report-on-h5n1-highly-pathogenic-avian-influenza-in-utah-mink-august-2026/1050"><b>our first detailed account</b></a></span> - posted on the <a href="http://Virological.org"><b>Virological.org</b></a> discussion forum - penned by researchers from the NIH, the Pirbright Institute, Imperial College, London, and Sorbonne Université.&nbsp;</div></blockquote><div><br />Since this is not explicitly listed as available under a <b>creative commons license</b> (<i>there is very old CC 3.0 notice under terms of use)</i>, I'm going to only briefly summarize the findings, and urge my readers to follow<a href="https://virological.org/t/preliminary-report-on-h5n1-highly-pathogenic-avian-influenza-in-utah-mink-august-2026/1050"><b> the link</b></a> and read it in its entirety.&nbsp;<br /><br /></div><div style="text-align: left;">Briefly, the authors report that:&nbsp;</div><div><ul style="text-align: left;"><li>Based on <b>10 samples taken on Aug 7th </b>- the H5N1 virus detected was the `<b>Bovine' B3.13 </b>genotype. It carried the pre-existing cattle&nbsp;<b>PB2-M631L adaptation</b>, along with <b>NA mutations K432E</b> and<b> N434S.</b></li></ul><ul style="text-align: left;"><li><b>Of note</b>,<b>&nbsp;</b>all ten mink viruses carry <b>PB1-K388R</b>, which was seen in the 2022 Spanish mink outbreak, which is rarely seen in birds, and absent in cattle.&nbsp;</li></ul><ul style="text-align: left;"><li>The mink viruses most closely resemble the 2026 cattle clade <i>(Idaho, Texas, Utah</i>), with the closest match being Texas cattle viruses sampled May 28, 2026.</li></ul><ul style="text-align: left;"><li>The most recent common ancestor is estimated to date back to about<b> July 4</b> (95% HPD June 21–July 15), and suggests a single introduction followed by weeks of undetected spread.</li></ul><ul style="text-align: left;"><li>While wild birds were considered the most likely source of mink outbreaks in Spain and Finland, they report<i><span style="color: #2b00fe;">&nbsp;`. . . the transmission route between Texas cattle to Utah mink is considerably less clear.'</span></i></li></ul><ul style="text-align: left;"><li>Since only the Aug 7th sequences have been released, we don't know if additional mutations may have occurred.&nbsp; As of late September the outbreak was still reportedly ongoing, and no culling had been undertaken.&nbsp;</li></ul></div><p>The link to the full report follows. I'll have a brief postscript after the break.&nbsp;</p><div><a href="https://virological.org/t/preliminary-report-on-h5n1-highly-pathogenic-avian-influenza-in-utah-mink-august-2026/1050"></a><blockquote><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><a href="https://virological.org/t/preliminary-report-on-h5n1-highly-pathogenic-avian-influenza-in-utah-mink-august-2026/1050"><b><span style="font-size: large;">Preliminary report on H5N1 highly pathogenic avian influenza in Utah mink, August 2026</span></b></a> <br /><br /><a href="https://virological.org/c/influenza-virus/17">Influenza virus</a>&nbsp;<a href="https://virological.org/c/influenza-virus/h5n1-global/52">H5N1-global</a><br /><br /><a href="https://virological.org/t/preliminary-report-on-h5n1-highly-pathogenic-avian-influenza-in-utah-mink-august-2026/1050/1">Oct 22</a> <br />post by Martha_NIH 14 hours ago<br /><a href="https://virological.org/u/martha_nih"><img src="https://virological.org/letter_avatar_proxy/v4/letter/m/51bf81/48.png" /></a><br /><br /><a href="https://virological.org/u/martha_nih">Martha_NIH</a><br />&nbsp;<br />Alvin Crespo-Bellido1, Jennifer L. Havens1, Thomas P. Peacock2,3, Florence Débarre4, Martha I. Nelson1<br /><br /><span style="font-size: xx-small;">1 Division of Intramural Research, National Library of Medicine, National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD USA<br />2 The Pirbright Institute, Woking, UK<br />3Department of Infectious Disease, Imperial College London, UK<br />4 Institut d’Écologie et des Sciences de l’Environnement, CNRS, Sorbonne Université, UPEC, IRD, INRAE, Paris, France</span></span></blockquote><p>&nbsp;</p><p><span style="font-family: inherit;">During the height of  Finland's fur farm epizootic in 2023, we looked at an opinion piece by one of today's authors - </span><b style="font-family: inherit;">Thomas P. Peacock </b><span style="font-family: inherit;">(along with </span><a href="https://www.imperial.ac.uk/people/w.barclay" style="font-family: inherit;"><b>Professor Wendy Barclay</b></a><span style="font-family: inherit;">) - on why fur farms - </span><i style="font-family: inherit;">and mink farms in particular -</i><span style="font-family: inherit;"> are high-risk venues for novel flu.</span></p></div><blockquote style="border: none; margin: 0 0 0 40px; padding: 0px;"><div><h3 class="post-title entry-title" itemprop="name" style="background-color: #ebedec; color: #00007f; font-feature-settings: normal; font-kerning: auto; font-language-override: normal; font-optical-sizing: auto; font-size-adjust: none; font-stretch: normal; font-style: normal; font-variant: normal; font-variation-settings: normal; line-height: normal; margin: 0px; position: relative; text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: inherit; font-size: large;"><a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2023/07/pnas-mink-farming-poses-risks-for.html">PNAS: Mink Farming Poses Risks for Future Viral Pandemics</a></span></h3></div></blockquote><p><span style="font-family: inherit;">Six week ago, in&nbsp;</span><span style="font-family: inherit;"> </span><a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/09/the-lancet-regional-health-europe.html" style="font-family: inherit;"><b>The Lancet Regional Health Europe (Comment): If the EU is serious about One Health, it must ban fur farming</b></a><span style="font-family: inherit;">, we looked at a similar call to action.&nbsp;</span></p><blockquote style="border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; margin: 0px 0px 0px 40px; padding: 0px; text-align: left;">While some EU countries have taken steps to phase out or ban fur farming, the industry continues in many parts of the world, including China, Russia, the United States, Canada and parts of the EU.</blockquote><p>Whether we can summon the political will to do something about these risks before a genuine public health threat emerges, remains to be seen.&nbsp;&nbsp;</p></description><link>https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/10/virological-referral-preliminary-report.html</link><author>noreply@blogger.com (Michael Coston)</author></item><item><guid isPermaLink="false">tag:blogger.com,1999:blog-21247748.post-7718586556596760627</guid><pubDate>Thu, 22 Oct 2026 09:53:46 +0000</pubDate>2026-10-22T05:53:46.191-04:00<title>FAO: Call to Strengthen Prevention, Surveillance, and Preparedness against HPAI in Latin America and the Caribbean</title><description><p>&nbsp;<a href="https://openknowledge.fao.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/27c4f233-536a-4534-9fc5-e10501615e31/content"><img height="211" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjzzzg2FUF1by3IWng-RcQRRfmPnu2e4L6aPc5Pr0yCfUrLOxbcBRTN5z8FgoqHV2uJTX-YRBGD5zdDdlXqTbjaT_SqEoNJjrM-Ll-vGMIN3OC_JgSI1hZ95N82nmxaZbJSGC7JID9Iz7i3wLc-iTxXbInuKizSUoo_c5HHNH7QeENQyUVH_ih6UA/w400-h211/image.png" width="400" /></a><br /><br /></p><p>#19,383</p><p>Although HPAI H5 has reached nearly every corner of the world, reporting from many regions remains spotty at best. Sometimes this data is deliberately withheld for political or economic reasons, but often it is due to a lack of resources, or difficulties conducting surveillance in remote or uninhabited regions.&nbsp;</p><p>The FAO's map of 2025-2026 Global AIV activity illustrates these gaps:</p><p></p><div class="separator" style="clear: both; text-align: center;"><a href="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEi7_0kOaRh55gAwOQKjQwe3GHrrpLv282Cz7fCifIs4YJtjuxNvDHQNGU2qqY3fJAxDmXdNohfrk-aN525IFo4OjB54k5pB0-eSFth2sl2CCX-aiUBkDxckOpAAO-AVW_OPW5tLkWQmW_RRRMAjckpWCA82Cb8NxhwZ85jFevmi-RJm3q-cULP26Q/s1600/image.png" style="margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 1em;"><img alt="" data-original-height="862" data-original-width="953" height="362" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEi7_0kOaRh55gAwOQKjQwe3GHrrpLv282Cz7fCifIs4YJtjuxNvDHQNGU2qqY3fJAxDmXdNohfrk-aN525IFo4OjB54k5pB0-eSFth2sl2CCX-aiUBkDxckOpAAO-AVW_OPW5tLkWQmW_RRRMAjckpWCA82Cb8NxhwZ85jFevmi-RJm3q-cULP26Q/w400-h362/image.png" width="400" /></a></div><p>Large swaths of Asia, Africa, South and Central America, and Northern Canada are essentially a blank slate. Yet we know, based on bird migratory patterns <i>(flyways)</i>, that HPAI incursions almost certainly are occurring.&nbsp;</p><div class="separator" style="clear: both; text-align: center;"><img border="0" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgItt2aL75_pNyew7ntG-_vtZ8fj1RWw-EYxuM8vLLuk31iV6BqJKz65M-e8L8x7i29YlNgd5qcAqCprYDZg-Lvu6zwfMrPYagaV-OA9UH4u89Wrn0qRRJKqf3KAJe9Mep9xI9DAQ/?imgmax=800" /></div><p style="background-color: #ebedec; color: #363636; font-family: Arial, Tahoma, Helvetica, FreeSans, sans-serif; font-size: 16px;"></p><p></p><p style="background-color: #ebedec; color: #363636; font-family: Arial, Tahoma, Helvetica, FreeSans, sans-serif; font-size: 16px; text-align: center;">Major Global Migratory Flyways – Credit <a href="http://www.fao.org/" style="color: #3f3f7f; text-decoration: none;">FAO</a></p>Last week the FAO issued an alert to Latin American and Caribbean nations advising them to strengthen their surveillance for - and preparedness against - HPAI as the coming months are likely to see an increased risk for outbreaks.&nbsp;<div><p>Due to its length, I've only posted some excerpts. Follow the link to read the document in its entirety.&nbsp; I'll have a brief postscript after the break.</p><p><br /></p><span style="font-family: inherit; font-size: medium;"><b></b></span><blockquote><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><span style="font-family: inherit; font-size: medium;"><b><a href="https://openknowledge.fao.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/27c4f233-536a-4534-9fc5-e10501615e31/content">CALL TO STRENGTHEN PREVENTION, SURVEILLANCE AND PREPAREDNESS MEASURES AGAINST HIGH PATHOGENICITY AVIAN INFLUENZA IN&nbsp;LATIN AMERICA AND THE CARIBBEAN</a></b></span><br /></span><div><span style="color: #2b00fe;">16 October 2026</span></div><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><br /><br />Given the continued circulation of high pathogenicity avian influenza (HPAI) viruses in the Americas and the proximity of a period of increased&nbsp;risk associated with the seasonal movements of migratory wild birds from&nbsp;the northern hemisphere to Latin America and the Caribbean, <b>FAO calls&nbsp;on official veterinary services, public health authorities, poultry producers&nbsp;and other stakeholders involved in animal health to strengthen prevention,&nbsp;surveillance, early detection and response preparedness measures against&nbsp;this disease.</b></span><div><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><br />HPAI continues to pose a health threat to poultry, wildlife and potentially other animal species and people. Avian influenza A(H5) viruses have continued to circulate across the continent in 2026. More than 10&nbsp;countries in the Americas have reported over 1 000 outbreaks and cases in&nbsp;domestic, wild and mammalian animals, according to data from the World&nbsp;Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) and the countries.</span></div><div><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><br />Experience over the past few years shows that wild birds, particularly migratory waterbirds, can play an important role in the geographical spread of avian influenza viruses. The migration and concentration of birds from different geographical areas provide opportunities for virus circulation and can increase the risk of introduction of the virus into domestic bird populations. According to official WOAH data and analysis&nbsp;of FAO EMPRES-i+ data over the past few years, <b>HPAI outbreaks tend to&nbsp;increase from October and reach their highest levels during the following&nbsp;months.</b></span></div><div><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><br />For this reason, the coming period requires increased vigilance and preparedness, especially in countries, territories and areas along migratory&nbsp;routes, in wetlands, lagoons, coastal areas or other places where wild birds&nbsp;congregate, and in areas where poultry farms are located close to these&nbsp;environments.</span></div><div><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><br />Avian influenza is a highly contagious viral disease that mainly affects domestic and wild birds. However, during the current epidemiological situation, infections have also been identified in various species of terrestrial and marine mammals.</span></div><div><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><br /></span></div><div><div><span style="color: #2b00fe;">In addition, certain avian influenza viruses have zoonotic potential and&nbsp;</span><span style="color: #2b00fe;">can occasionally infect humans, mainly in situations of close contact and&nbsp;</span><span style="color: #2b00fe;">without adequate protection with infected animals or contaminated&nbsp;</span><span style="color: #2b00fe;">environments. Although the risk to the general population is still considered low, surveillance should be maintained, especially among people with occupational or frequent exposure to potentially infected animals (Pan American Health Organization, (Pan American Health Organization, PAHO).</span></div><div><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><br /></span></div><div><span style="color: #2b00fe;">Based on the FAO-WOAH Global strategy for the prevention and control&nbsp;</span><span style="color: #2b00fe;">of high pathogenicity avian influenza (2024-2033) – Achieving sustainable, resilient poultry production systems, the FAO Regional Office for Latin America and the Caribbean provides specific recommendations for veterinary services and poultry producers.</span></div></div></blockquote><blockquote><div><div><a href="https://openknowledge.fao.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/27c4f233-536a-4534-9fc5-e10501615e31/content"><b>(Continue . . . )</b></a></div></div></blockquote><p>&nbsp;</p><p>While it is impossible to achieve anything approaching 100% surveillance, the more information we can gather and share, the less likely we are to be blindsided by an abrupt evolutionary change in the virus.&nbsp;</p><p>But whether that is enough of an incentive to see real change in the amount and quality of global surveillance and reporting on HPAI remains to be seen.&nbsp; &nbsp;</p></div><div><div><div></div></div></div></description><link>https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/10/fao-call-to-strengthen-prevention.html</link><author>noreply@blogger.com (Michael Coston)</author></item><item><guid isPermaLink="false">tag:blogger.com,1999:blog-21247748.post-415761874560958519</guid><pubDate>Wed, 21 Oct 2026 10:22:56 +0000</pubDate>2026-10-21T07:50:27.067-04:00<title>Washington State: Updated guidance for novel influenza screening and influenza subtyping</title><description><p>&nbsp;<a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/05/mmwr-fatal-human-case-of-hpai-ah5n5-in.html"><img src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjuZlu-oVTEKdA_po3nS9OYeHnPErEwgY6qqYU4Ub16SHdkV09GbwXGjIJKtIdHji36hxlAvl6jpNMeBeVis9IxHhtiC-AejeY0uVAIGO9AE7ziMYwLPYkZ5qvAoHW4Sh7oAt5FoOJew6SrdVyTewe4X3a7F6Pgubrw2zTgJmYvkyI6tvxpY_8HJQ/s1600/image.png" /></a><br /></p><span style="font-size: xx-small;"><a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/05/mmwr-fatal-human-case-of-hpai-ah5n5-in.html"><b>MMWR: Fatal Human Case of HPAI A(H5N5) in a Backyard Flock Owner</b></a></span><div><span style="font-size: xx-small;"><a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/05/mmwr-fatal-human-case-of-hpai-ah5n5-in.html"><b>&nbsp;— Washington, November 2025</b></a></span><p>#19,381</p><p>In November of 2025, Washington State reported the first known human infection with avian H5N5; a diagnosis that was delayed - according to <a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/05/mmwr-fatal-human-case-of-hpai-ah5n5-in.html"><b>an MMWR report</b></a> - by&nbsp;&nbsp;<i><b><span style="color: #2b00fe;">`early and repeated <u>negative influenza test results</u> from upper respiratory swab specimens'</span></b></i>.</p></div><blockquote style="border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; border: none; margin: 0px 0px 0px 40px; padding: 0px;"><div style="text-align: left;">As we've previously discussed, it takes a certain amount of luck for novel flu infections to be detected, properly treated, and then reported to the CDC.&nbsp;&nbsp;</div></blockquote><div><br /></div><div>The problem being that standard rapid influenza tests don't distinguish between seasonal and novel flu strains, and sometimes, repeated swabs of the upper airway can fail to <i>`capture'</i> a deep lung infection for RT-PCR testing.&nbsp;</div><div><br /></div><blockquote style="border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; border: none; margin: 0px 0px 0px 40px; padding: 0px;"><div style="text-align: left;">In the H5N5 case above, the patient died. In 2024, a Missouri patient was hospitalized with influenza A, and released, before being notified they had H5N1&nbsp;(see <a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2024/09/missouri-dhss-human-h5-bird-flu-case.html"><b>Missouri DHSS: Human H5 bird flu case confirmed in Missouri</b></a>).  In both cases, numerous hospital workers (and others) were unknowingly exposed.</div></blockquote><p>How many novel flu infections go undetected is unknown, although numerous studies suggest it happens more than we think (see <a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2025/11/jama-open-asymptomatic-human-infections.html"><b>JAMA Open: Asymptomatic Human Infections With Avian Influenza A(H5N1) Virus Confirmed by Molecular and Serologic Testing</b></a>&nbsp; and&nbsp;&nbsp;<b><a href=" https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2024/11/mmwr-serologic-evidence-of-recent.html">MMWR: Serologic Evidence of Recent Infection with HPAI A(H5) Virus Among Dairy Workers</a>)</b>.</p><blockquote style="border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; border: none; margin: 0px 0px 0px 40px; padding: 0px;"><p style="text-align: left;">No screening system can be expected to catch every case (<i>and many mild cases simply won't seek medical care</i>), but a standardized screening procedure can improve the chances.&nbsp;</p></blockquote><p>Yesterday <a href="https://kingcounty.gov/"><b>King County, Washington</b></a> published updated guidance for screening for novel influenza, following last week's report of a<b><a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/10/washington-state-confirms-human-avian.html"> dairy-exposure infection in Yakima county.</a></b>&nbsp; This appears to be a condensed version of guidance published by the  WA State Dept. of Health <b>(<a href="https://doh.wa.gov/sites/default/files/2026-10/ProviderAlert-FluTestingSubtyping-Sept2026.pdf">Provider Alert: Testing and Subtyping for Avian Influenza</a>)</b> published on Oct 9th.&nbsp;</p><blockquote style="border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; border: none; margin: 0px 0px 0px 40px; padding: 0px;"><div style="text-align: left;">The emphasis here is on testing patients with <b>ARI </b>(Acute Respiratory Illness) with recent (<i>past 10 days)</i><b> epidemiologic risk factors</b> (<i>poultry/livestock exposure, raw dairy or animal products, known contact with a human case, etc.</i>).&nbsp;</div></blockquote><div><br /></div><div>It should be noted that this criteria would not have targeted the <a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2024/12/nejm-critical-illness-in-adolescent.html"><b>BC teenager with H5N1</b></a>, the <a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2024/09/missouri-dhss-human-h5-bird-flu-case.html"><b>Missouri case</b></a> mentioned above, and several others whose source of exposure remains unknown.&nbsp;</div><div><br /></div><div><div class="separator" style="clear: both; text-align: center;"><a href="https://www.cdc.gov/bird-flu/situation-summary/" style="margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 1em;"><img alt="" data-original-height="239" data-original-width="326" height="235" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgTgwlABDEaL7LACu4eZLQNIFZg4czIcZ69h8ZUfg1axELdiEkzsppcNDj4KxYMiCq7fnx68pgMCgpaxwp8J2UWEV7nl1aT9nqTAsz_sZrmk8k0Jf9HDsGMTPkD354oq7vTE4U3F1aWtooVWOhPfD7z6zldO0W2CTxRbofAFYni7tFrUHVudfdGnw/s1600/image.png" width="320" /></a></div><span style="font-size: x-small;"><div style="text-align: center;"><a href="https://www.cdc.gov/bird-flu/situation-summary/"><b>Credit CDC</b></a></div></span><br /></div><div>In early 2025, the CDC issued a&nbsp;<a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2025/01/cdc-han-accelerated-subtyping-of.html" style="font-feature-settings: normal; font-kerning: auto; font-language-override: normal; font-optical-sizing: auto; font-size-adjust: none; font-stretch: normal; font-variant-alternates: normal; font-variant-east-asian: normal; font-variant-emoji: normal; font-variant-numeric: normal; font-variant-position: normal; font-variation-settings: normal; line-height: normal;"><b>HAN: Accelerated Subtyping of Influenza A in Hospitalized Patients</b></a>, requesting that all hospitalized patients with suspected influenza be subtyped within 24 hours.&nbsp;&nbsp;</div><div><br /></div><blockquote style="border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; border: none; margin: 0px 0px 0px 40px; padding: 0px;"><div style="text-align: left;">Today's guidance appears to back away from that, although the reason behind that isn't stated.&nbsp;&nbsp;</div></blockquote><p>Based on the CDC's analysis of 72 human cases since 2024, however, it does appear that the vast majority of known cases had some kind of animal exposure.&nbsp;</p><p>I've reproduced the King County Guidance below, followed by a link to the WA State provider update.&nbsp; I'll have a postscript after the break.</p><div><br /><blockquote><span style="color: #2b00fe;">October 20, 2026<br /><br /><b><span style="font-size: large;"><a href="https://kingcounty.gov/en/dept/dph/health-safety/disease-illness/health-advisories/2026/10-20-novel-flu-screening-subtyping">Updated guidance for novel influenza screening and influenza subtyping</a></span></b><br /><br />➜ <b><a href="https://cdn.kingcounty.gov/-/media/king-county/depts/dph/documents/health-safety/disease-illness/advisories/2026/health-advisory-october-20-2026.pdf?rev=0c7728ce6aa4469ca171c3291f7d6989&amp;hash=113CFC5459196189CC11652CE092FAC2&amp;_gl=1*1n3ooxv*_ga*Njg4NDI1Nzk2LjE3OTI1NzE4OTE.*_ga_W2BH6TXD2Z*czE3OTI1NzE4OTAkbzEkZzEkdDE3OTI1NzIxMjQkajQzJGwwJGgw">This health advisory is also available in PDF format</a> (</b>223 KB)<br /><br /><b>Current situation</b><br /><br />Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI or bird flu) continues to circulate among wild birds and other animals in Washington. Although the risk to the general public remains low, clinicians should remain vigilant for possible avian influenza infections in patients with acute respiratory illness (ARI) and epidemiologic risk factors.<br /><br /><b><a href="https://doh.wa.gov/sites/default/files/2026-10/ProviderAlert-FluTestingSubtyping-Sept2026.pdf">Guidance has changed for the 2026-27 influenza season</a>,</b> summarized below.<br /></span></blockquote><blockquote><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><b><span style="font-size: medium;">Actions requested</span></b><br /><br /><b>Identify</b></span><div><ul style="text-align: left;"><li><span style="color: #2b00fe;">Test all patients with <b>ARI AND epidemiologic risk factors</b> for influenza and obtain seasonal influenza subtyping for influenza A-positive specimens. Epidemiologic risk factors include the following within <b>10 days</b> before symptom onset:</span></li></ul></div></blockquote><blockquote><ul style="text-align: left;"><ul><li><span style="color: #2b00fe;">Close contact with sick or dead animals or their environments, especially birds, wildlife, livestock (including poultry), or domestic animals suspected of HPAI</span></li><li><span style="color: #2b00fe;">Consumption or handling of raw animal products or parts from potentially infected animals (e.g., raw cow milk or products made with it, raw meat-based pet food)</span></li><li><span style="color: #2b00fe;">Close contact (within 6 feet) to someone suspected or confirmed to have avian influenza</span></li></ul><li><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><u>Influenza A subtyping is <b>NOT</b> requested for patients without epidemiologic risk factors, including hospitalized patients</u>.
