color: #363636; font-family: Arial, Tahoma, Helvetica, FreeSans, sans-serif; font-size: 16px;">Photo Credit <a href="http://www3.niaid.nih.gov/" style="color: #3f3f7f; text-decoration: none;">NIAID</a></div><p>#19,378</p><p>While it doesn't get near the attention it did before COVID, MERS-CoV continues to circulate in dromedary camels in the Middle East, occasionally spills over into humans, and is likely under reported.&nbsp; &nbsp;</p><blockquote style="border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; border: none; margin: 0px 0px 0px 40px; padding: 0px;"><p style="text-align: left;">MERS-CoV also continues to evolve, which raises concerns over its future impact (see<b>&nbsp;<a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2025/10/health-sci-rpts-narrative-review.html">Health Sci Rpts (Narrative Review): Pathogenicity and Potential Role of MERS-CoV in the Emergence of “Disease X”</a>). </b></p></blockquote>In 2025, the WHO released 3 MERS-CoV DON reports (see <b><a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2025/12/who-don-middle-east-respiratory.html">here</a>, <a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2025/05/who-saudi-arabia-reports-9-new-mers-cov.html">here</a></b>, and <b><a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2025/03/who-don-middle-east-respiratory.html">here</a></b>), and last December, France reported <b><a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2025/12/france-moh-2-travelers-returning-from.html">2 </a><a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2025/12/france-moh-2-travelers-returning-from.html">Travelers Returning From Arabian Peninsula Diagnosed with the MERS-CoV</a></b> virus.<p>This year has been somewhat quieter, with the first WHO update of 2026 published just last week (October 15th), which chronicles <b>8 cases</b> reported by Saudi Arabia since last December.&nbsp;&nbsp;</p><blockquote style="border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; border: none; margin: 0px 0px 0px 40px; padding: 0px;"><p>Of note - while the WHO states&nbsp;<span style="color: #2b00fe;">`<b>Humans contract MERS-CoV through direct or indirect contact with dromedary camels, the virus’s natural host and zoonotic reservoir.</b></span>'  - <b>6 of the 8 cases</b> reported<b>&nbsp;no known contact with camels or camel products.&nbsp;</b></p></blockquote><p>This is not a new trend; in 2025 more than half of the cases reported by KSA listed no known contact with camels or camel products, and this&nbsp;<a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2022/01/saudi-arabia-announces-4-additional.html"><b>has been frequently reported in the past.</b></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p><blockquote style="border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; margin: 0px 0px 0px 40px; padding: 0px; text-align: left;"><p>Exactly how these people are contracting the virus remains unclear.&nbsp;&nbsp;</p></blockquote><p>First some excerpts from the latest DON report, after which I'll have a postscript.</p><blockquote style="border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; margin: 0px 0px 0px 40px; padding: 0px;"><br /><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><b><span style="font-size: large;"><a href="https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/middle-east-respiratory-syndrome-coronavirus---kingdom-of-saudi-arabia">Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus - Kingdom of Saudi Arabia</a></span><br /><span style="font-size: medium;">15 October 2026</span></b><br /><br /><b>Situation at a glance</b><br /></span></blockquote><blockquote style="border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; border: none; margin: 0px 0px 0px 40px; padding: 0px;"><p style="text-align: left;"><span style="color: #2b00fe;">&nbsp;Between 1 January and 5 October 2026, the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia reported eight laboratory-confirmed cases of Middle East Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus (MERS-CoV) infection, including one death. Cases were detected across six locations: Al Jouf (1), Arar (1), Hafr Al-Batin (1), Riyadh (2), Tabuk (1) and Taif (2). No epidemiological links were identified between any of the cases. All eight cases were symptomatic, most commonly presenting with fever (6/8), dyspnea (5/8), and cough (4/8). None were health and care workers. Infection was confirmed by RT-PCR testing. MERS is a zoonotic viral respiratory disease for which dromedary camels serve as the primary animal reservoir and <b>two cases reported direct contact with camels while six reported no known camel exposure</b>. Seven of eight cases had underlying comorbidities, recognized risk factors for severe MERS-CoV disease. The cases appear to represent sporadic infections related to zoonotic spillover rather than a single outbreak cluster.</span></p></blockquote><blockquote style="border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; margin: 0px 0px 0px 40px; padding: 0px;"><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><b>Description of the situation</b><br /><br />Between 1 January and 5 October 2026, a total of eight cases of MERS-CoV, including one death, was reported from six locations in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. Of the eight reported cases, five occurred among persons aged 70 years and older, two among adults aged 50–59 years, and one among an adult aged 30–39 years. Seven cases had underlying comorbidities, two reported direct camel contact, and one death was reported in an older adult (&gt;65 year old) with comorbidities. There was no known epidemiological link identified among cases.<br /><br />Case 1: A male aged 50–59 years, with comorbidities, from Al Jouf developed symptoms on 14 March 2026. He reported <b>no known contact with camels or camel products. </b>The patient was hospitalized on 17 March and laboratory confirmation of MERS-CoV infection was obtained by RT-PCR on 19 March.<br /><br />Case 2: A male aged ≥70 years, with comorbidities, from Taif developed symptoms on 18 April 2026. He reported <b>no known contact with camels or camel products</b>. The patient was hospitalized on the same day, and laboratory confirmation was obtained on 22 April. He subsequently died as a result of the illness.<br /><br />Case 3: A male aged ≥70 years, with comorbidities, from Hafr Al-Batin developed symptoms on 20 May 2026.<b> <u>He reported direct contact with camels</u></b>. The patient was hospitalized on 26 May and laboratory confirmation was obtained on 27 May.<br /><br />Case 4: A female aged ≥70 years, with comorbidities, from Riyadh developed symptoms on 31 July 2026. <b>No known exposure to camels or camel products</b> was reported. She was hospitalized on 3 August and laboratory confirmation was obtained on 8 August.<br /><br />Case 5: A male aged 50–59 years, with comorbidities, from Tabuk developed symptoms on 20 August 2026. He reported <b>no known contact with camels or camel products</b>. He was hospitalized on 23 August and laboratory confirmation was obtained by RT-PCR on 24 August.<br /><br />Case 6: A male aged 30–39 years, with no known comorbidities, from Riyadh developed symptoms on 14 August 2026.<b> He reported no known contact with camels or camel products.</b> He was hospitalized on 20 August and laboratory confirmation was obtained on 23 August.<br /><br />Case 7: A male aged ≥70 years, with comorbidities, from Taif developed symptoms on 11 September 2026. He reported <b>no known contact with camels or camel products.</b> He was hospitalized on 17 September and laboratory confirmation was obtained on 19 September.<br /><br />Case 8: A male aged 60–69 years, with comorbidities, from Arar developed symptoms on 20 September 2026. <u><b>He reported direct contact with camels</b></u>. He was hospitalized on 20 September and laboratory confirmation was obtained on 21 September.</span></blockquote><p>&nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; <b><span style="color: #2b00fe;">(SNIP)</span></b></p><b><span style="color: #2b00fe;"></span></b><blockquote><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><b>WHO risk assessment</b><br /><br />MERS is a zoonotic viral respiratory disease caused by MERS-CoV, for which dromedary camels serve as the primary animal reservoir. Human infection can range from asymptomatic or mild illness to severe disease and death. Human infections continue to occur through direct or indirect exposure to infected dromedaries or their products, while limited human-to-human transmission has been documented, primarily among close contacts and in healthcare settings. Sustained community transmission has not been observed. No licensed vaccine for MERS-CoV exists to date.<br /><br />As of 5 October 2026, WHO had been notified of 2<b>643 laboratory-confirmed MERS cases globally, including 965 deaths, since the virus was first identified in 2012. </b>The majority of cases (84%; 2232 cases and 870 deaths) have been reported from Saudi Arabia<b>. These figures likely underestimate the true number of infections since mild and asymptomatic cases may remain undetected/unreported, while the reported case fatality of ratio of 37% may overestimate mortality among infections.</b><br /><br />Although the number of reported MERS cases has declined substantially since 2020, MERS-CoV continues to circulate in dromedary camel populations in the Middle East and African regions and continues to cause sporadic human infections. The observed decline in reported MERS cases, in particular during the COVID-19 pandemic emergency phase, is thought to be a result of pandemic-related IPC measures that also limited human-to-human transmission of MERS-CoV, as well as behavioral changes during the pandemic. Any role of potential cross-reactive immunity from SARS-CoV-2 infection and/ or vaccination remains in need of further investigation. Other hypotheses—such as reduced surveillance, viral attenuation, or decreased circulation in camel populations—are not supported by current evidence.<br /><br />WHO expects additional sporadic MERS cases to occur in countries where the virus circulates in camels and anticipates that travel-associated exportation of cases will continue. Delays in detection remain possible due to the clinical presentation of MERS being similar with other respiratory infections, including influenza and COVID-19. Numerous outbreaks <a href="https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/12-june-2015-mers-korea-en">in KSA and the Republic of Korea</a> have demonstrated that primary cases can result in substantial secondary transmission, particularly in healthcare settings and through importation of travel related cases.<br /><br />The notification of the recent cases in Saudi Arabia does not change WHO's overall risk assessment -  the<b> risk remains moderate at both the regional and global levels</b>, reflecting the continued occurrence of sporadic zoonotic infections, the potential for healthcare-associated outbreaks and international exportation of cases, in the absence of sustained human-to-human transmission.<br /><br />WHO continues to monitor the epidemiological situation through routine surveillance and reporting under the International Health Regulations (IHR 2005) and conducts ongoing risk assessments using available epidemiological and virological information.</span></blockquote><p><span style="color: #2b00fe;">&nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp;<a href="https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/middle-east-respiratory-syndrome-coronavirus---kingdom-of-saudi-arabia"> <b>&nbsp;(Continue . . . )</b></a></span></p><blockquote style="border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; border: none; margin: 0px 0px 0px 40px; padding: 0px;"></blockquote><p>In June of 2025 we looked at an editorial in<b> <a href="https://link.springer.com/journal/44197">Journal of Epidemiology &amp; Global Health</a></b>  on the importance of <b>healthcare preparedness and surveillance</b> (see <b><a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2025/06/jegh-al-tawfiq-memish-on-recurrent-mers.html">Al-Tawfiq &amp; Memish On Recurrent MERS-CoV Transmission in Saudi Arabia</a>)</b>, with an emphasis on identifying<b> <span style="color: #990000;"><u>asymptomatic carriers</u>.</span></b>&nbsp;</p><blockquote style="border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; border: none; margin: 0px 0px 0px 40px; padding: 0px;"><div style="text-align: left;"><span style="font-family: inherit;">Two months later we reviewed an&nbsp;</span><a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2025/08/ijid-editorial-al-tawfiq-on-global.html" style="font-family: inherit;"><b>IJID Editorial: Al-Tawfiq on Global Epidemiology and Public Health Challenges of Middle East Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus (MERS-CoV)</b></a><span style="font-family: inherit;"> - which looked again at what may be the most challenging aspect of MERS detection; </span><span style="color: #990000; font-family: inherit; font-weight: bold;">asymptomatic </span><span style="font-family: inherit;">or </span><span style="color: #990000; font-family: inherit; font-weight: bold;">mildly symptomatic cases.</span></div></blockquote><p>Although MERS-CoV clearly isn't ready for prime time, each new zoonotic spillover from camels - <i>or cryptic transmission</i> - is another opportunity for the virus to better adapt to a human host.&nbsp;&nbsp;</p><p style="text-align: left;">Which is why we need better MERS-CoV surveillance and reporting, both in the Middle East, and in Africa (see<b>  <a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2018/06/eid-journal-geographic-distribution-of.html">EID Journal: Geographic Distribution of MERS-CoV among Dromedary Camels, Africa</a>).</b>&nbsp;</p></description><link>https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/10/who-don-middle-east-respiratory.html</link><author>noreply@blogger.com (Michael Coston)</author></item><item><guid text-align: center;"><a href="https://doh.wa.gov/you-and-your-family/illness-and-disease-z/bird-flu" style="margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 1em;"><img alt="" data-original-height="822" data-original-width="1005" height="328" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgLm3XDY6xc9AxwsIk6NbhsfoRy60gJakuZv0jR9bQTXlVX_OezMmo0Kge5SLcuz2nMigo1eAoFOhoUQAMqEdAnZxhn1sVHZIH35JRQ85Adx-5M9h2A24kyRLFefK39DlQ-HrCoTHBCVgDtOkpOgz8Ma1oDrBPTYLLxDW_1sHH3BhjsYsGtOWE7OA/w400-h328/image.png" width="400" /></a></div><br />While recommended, the use of PPEs has been suboptimal, particularly on farms and ranches. border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; margin: 0px 0px 0px 40px; padding: 0px; text-align: left;"><a href="https://americanpetproducts.org/news/the-american-pet-products-association-appa-releases-2025-state-of-the-industry-report"><b>The APPA estimates</b></a> `Eleven (11) million U.S. households own backyard chickens (<i>a 28% increase from 2023</i>)', yet a recent survey (see<b> <a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/05/mmwr-knowledge-attitudes-and-practices.html">MMWR: Knowledge, Attitudes, and Practices Regarding Avian Influenza Among Owners of Backyard Flocks</a></b>) found significant gaps in their knowledge of dealing with avian flu.&nbsp;</blockquote><p style="background-color: #ebedec; color: #363636; font-family: Arial, Tahoma, Helvetica, FreeSans, sans-serif; font-size: 16px; text-align: center;"><img border="0" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhGaN8aojnVVCTqlZIrEdp4OfDEI714-a-bziJP6G2MJiceLP97TIhTwtevxvp2JnZq6KlV_12_Pfiz5mKSa3hlWv-TCoGch-P7kMg7fHoWLzUkLLpp8frxxAMz2aqnbcT6HUu8NA/s400/CDC+Bird+flu+prevention.JPG" style="background: transparent; border-radius: 0px; border: 1px solid transparent; box-shadow: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.2) 0px 0px 0px; padding: 8px;" /></p>Although it is too early to predict what kind of avian flu season we will see this fall and winter - or whether<b><a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2025/08/h5nx-reassort-repeat.html"> any new genotypes</a>&nbsp;</b>will be added to the mix - we are already<b><a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/10/nevada-dept-of-wildlife-warns-on-hpai.html"> seeing signs of increased activity.</a></b>&nbsp;&nbsp;<div><br /></div><div>Which means, if you raise backyard birds, frequent live markets, or have outdoor pets, now would be a good time to familiarize yourselves with the risks of avian flu, and the things you can do to reduce those risks to you and your families.<br /><div style="background-color: #ebedec; font-kerning: auto; font-language-override: normal; font-optical-sizing: auto; font-size-adjust: none; font-stretch: normal; font-variant-alternates: normal; font-variant-east-asian: normal; font-variant-emoji: normal; font-variant-numeric: normal; font-variant-position: normal; font-variation-settings: normal; line-height: normal;"><b>Washington state confirmed their first detection of avian influenza in dairy cattle</b></a>, and overnight it was announced by the <b>Yakima County Health District</b> that a local resident who was exposed to infected dairy cows has tested positive for the virus.</p><blockquote style="border: none; margin: 0 0 0 40px; padding: 0px;"><p style="text-align: left;">There is still a lot we don't know about this case, hopefully the CDC will provide more details later today in their weekly FluView.&nbsp; &nbsp;</p></blockquote><p>The full press release follows.&nbsp; I'll update this report as more information becomes available.</p><b><span style="font-size: large;"></span></b><blockquote><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><b><span style="font-size: large;"><a href="https://www.yakimacounty.us/2417/Media-Releases#docaccess-9da5cc1738194b3305738e318406f325">Yakima County Resident Tests Positive for Avian Influenza</a></span></b><br /><br />We Are Public Health<br /><br /><b>Media Release</b><br /><br />For immediate release: October 15, 2026<br /><br />Contact: Stephanie Ruiz, Communications Specialist (509) 941-7364<br /><br />Yakima County Resident Tests Positive for Avian Influenza<br /><br />Yakima, WA- The Yakima Health District (YHD), in coordination with the Washington State Department of Health (DOH), is reporting a <b>confirmed case of avian influenza</b> in a Yakima County resident who was <b>exposed to <a href="https://www.yakimacounty.us/2417/Media-Releases#docaccess-51e51115f46ea8130711558d44e1682d">infected dairy cattle at a Yakima County dairy</a></b>. The resident has not experienced severe illness or been hospitalized. The individual is isolating at home.<br /><br />The risk of avian influenza infection to the general public remains low. People at greater risk include dairy workers and others who have close or prolonged contact with infected animals or environments contaminated with the virus. Transmission of avian influenza between humans is extremely rare and has never been documented in the United States. To ensure that human-to-human spread is not occurring, public health officials are contacting anyone who has been in close contact with the patient to monitor for symptoms.<br /><br />Since the initial detection of Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) H5N1 in Yakima County, YHD has been in contact with the impacted dairies to protect the health of people who may be exposed to infected cattle.<br /><br />YHD continues to coordinate with state and federal public health partners to provide guidance and resources to help protect exposed individuals. This includes providing tests for exposed individuals who develop symptoms to support prompt diagnosis and appropriate medical care. YHD is working with partners to connect affected dairies with appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE) for their workers.<br />About Avian Influenza<br /><br />Avian influenza, commonly called bird flu, is caused by influenza viruses that primarily circulate among wild birds but can also infect other animals, including poultry and dairy cattle. On rare occasions, these viruses infect people and cause illness.<br /><br />Most human infections with avian influenza have occurred following close or prolonged contact with infected animals or environments contaminated with the virus. People can become infected when virus enters their eyes, nose, or mouth. The severity of illness can range from mild to serious and potentially life-threatening.<br /></span></blockquote><blockquote><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><b>Public Health Recommendations</b><br /><br />The risk of avian influenza infection to the general public is low. However, people who work with or have contact with potentially infected animals are at higher risk and should follow workplace safety guidance and use recommended <a href="https://doh.wa.gov/you-and-your-family/illness-and-disease-z/bird-flu#protect">personal protective equipment</a>. Residents should avoid touching sick or dead animals, animal waste, and surfaces that may be contaminated.<br /><br />Pasteurized milk and dairy products remain safe to consume. Pasteurization inactivates avian influenza virus and other harmful pathogens. People should avoid raw milk and unpasteurized dairy products because they may contain harmful germs, including avian influenza. Do not feed pets raw milk, unpasteurized dairy products, or raw meat, including raw pet foods.<br /><br /><b>It is especially important that people who may have exposure to sick animals get a seasonal flu vaccine.</b> While the seasonal flu vaccine will not prevent bird flu infection, it reduces the risk of becoming sick with both human and avian influenza viruses at the same time. Seasonal flu vaccine is recommended for everyone six months and older.<br /><br />Symptoms of avian influenza in people can include eye redness or irritation, fever or feeling feverish, cough, sore throat, runny or stuffy nose, muscle or body aches, headache, and fatigue. More severe illness can occur.<br /><br />If you work on a dairy farm and develop symptoms after potential exposure to infected cattle, contact your healthcare provider or the Yakima Health District at <a href="tel:+15092496541">(509) 249-6541</a>.<br />Reporting Sick or Dead Animals<br /><br /><b>Domestic Birds</b>:Report sick/dead domestic birds using the <a href="https://arcg.is/05KT8S">online form</a>, or call the Washington State Department of Agriculture’s Avian Health Program: <a href="tel:+18006063056">1-800-606-3056</a>. Visit <a href="https://agr.wa.gov/birdflu">Avian Influenza |</a> <a href="https://agr.wa.gov/birdflu">Washington State Department of Agriculture</a> for more information about how to protect backyard flocks.<br /><br /><b>Wild Birds:</b>Use an <a href="https://survey123.arcgis.com/share/a384e90f69744f2e846135a9ce80027f">online form</a> to report sick/dead wild birds suspected of avian influenza to the <a href="https://wdfw.wa.gov/species-habitats/diseases/bird-flu">Washington Department of Fish &amp; Wildlife</a>.<br /><br /><b>Livestock</b>: To report sick livestock, isolate affected animals and contact your veterinarian and WSDA at 360-902-1878 or email <a href="mailto:ahealth@agr.wa.gov">ahealth@agr.wa.gov</a>.<br /></span></blockquote><blockquote><span style="color: #2b00fe;"><b>Quote</b><br /><br /><b><i>“We are working closely with our public health partners to follow up with people who have been in close contact with this individual. We want to make sure they know what symptoms to watch for and can access testing and treatment if needed.</i>”</b> -Dr. Dave Atteberry, Health Officer, Yakima Health District&nbsp;</span></blockquote></description><link>https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/10/washington-state-confirms-human-avian.html</link><author>noreply@blogger.com (Michael Coston)</author></item><item><guid isPermaLink="false">tag:blogger.com,1999:blog-21247748.post-6705236608021269373</guid><pubDate>Thu, 15 Oct 2026 10:33:28 +0000</pubDate>2026-10-15T06:33:28.323-04:00<title>Australia: H5 Bird Flu Reported on Macquarie Island</title><description><p>&nbsp;<img height="274" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhflwgBTJKui4rSCCqs59IIh-KG0mrCW3Gu9xzwBL44PXMVTT9lu32fg_65HbVl3_kUcj8SdkLIGFFvFb70dCjxdeqBt8gBJp9gXUu50DtHsUCKyZ8dEvalzXeXNHihkZ-4I-0SXz3dNjw7uux1pP5XaGeRZiMT7RnQh6Tqa767A3wDXnaiUOTmLA/w320-h274/image.png" width="320" /><br /><span style="font-size: xx-small;">Macquarie Island - Credit Wikipedia</span></p><p>#19,375</p><p>Six weeks ago Australia announced they would soon be&nbsp;<b><a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/08/australia-h5n1-sa-confirms-h5n1-in-red.html">withdrawing their research team from remote Macquarie Island</a></b> - located about halfway between Australia and Antarctica - over concerns that bird flu would arrive and decimate that island's wildlife much as it did on<b> <a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2025/10/australia-daff-dcceew-suspected-h5-bird.html">Heard Island</a></b> last year.&nbsp;</p><blockquote style="border-color: currentcolor; border-image: none; border-style: none; border-width: medium; margin: 0px 0px 0px 40px; padding: 0px; text-align: left;">Citing `<i>psychosocial risks' </i>to personnel who were stationed there, <a href="https://www.dcceew.gov.au/"><b>DCCEEW</b></a> decided to temporarily extract all personnel from the research station.</blockquote><p>Today, Guy Barnett, Tasmanian Minister for Environment and Climate Change, announced that the evacuated research team brought back with them samples from the island which have tested positive for H5 bird flu.<br /><br /></p><blockquote><span style="color: #2b00fe;"> 15 October 2026<br /><br />Guy Barnett, Minister for Environment and Climate Change<br /><br /><a href="https://www.premier.tas.gov.au/latest-news/2026/october/h5-bird-flu-detected-on-macquarie-island"><span style="font-size: medium;"><b>H5 bird flu has been detected in a Southern elephant seal and a kelp gull on Macquarie Island.</b></span></a><br /><br />Samples collected from a<b> Southern elephant seal</b> and a <b>kelp gull</b> on Macquarie Island were returned with island personnel and subsequently tested returning a positive result for H5 bird flu.<br /><br /><b>This is the first recorded detection in a marine mammal in Tasmania.</b><br /><br />As bird flu continues to be detected in Tasmania, members of the public are encouraged to continue reporting sick or dead birds. Reports play an important role in helping authorities detect and respond to potential cases.<br /><br />Avoid contact with sick or dead birds and report sightings through <a href="https://aus01.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fctrk.klclick.com%2Fl%2F01M4YXXKBDVSN0W7DXZ58SP17G_0&amp;data=05%7C02%7Cthomas.bearman%40dpac.tas.gov.au%7C237694258a5d4561d62c08df2a76cdcc%7Cea732b1f3d1a4be9b48b6cee25b8a074%7C0%7C0%7C639276361907077817%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&amp;sdata=hjdzHc9nFeusyw9fGWKTU3RdZyYrxqsgTse6fVJbFFY%3D&amp;reserved=0">https://nre.tas.gov.au/reportbirdflu</a> or by calling the Emergency Animal Disease Hotline on 1800 675 888.<br /><br />The Department of Natural Resources and Environment Tasmania provides regular public updates through media releases. The latest testing and surveillance figures are updated on the department's website.<br /><br />More information is available at  <a href="https://aus01.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fctrk.klclick.com%2Fl%2F01M4YXXKBDVSN0W7DXZ58SP17G_1&amp;data=05%7C02%7Cthomas.bearman%40dpac.tas.gov.au%7C237694258a5d4561d62c08df2a76cdcc%7Cea732b1f3d1a4be9b48b6cee25b8a074%7C0%7C0%7C639276361907119297%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&amp;sdata=y4RPLcHpWuSQ85za4xz0qVF1YUlIHiqyAaR5eVRrinA%3D&amp;reserved=0">www.nre.tas.gov.au/BirdFlu</a>.</span></blockquote><p><br />While there are no reports of mass casualties on Macquarie Island, four months ago, in&nbsp;<a href="https://afludiary.blogspot.com/2026/06/preprint-mass-mortality-of-southern.html"><b>Preprint: Mass mortality of southern elephant seals during multi-species outbreak of HPAI H5N1 on sub-Antarctic Heard Island</b></a>,&nbsp;we saw that the carnage<span style="background-color: #ebedec; color: #363636; font-family: Arial, Tahoma, Helvetica, FreeSans, sans-serif; font-size: 16px;">&nbsp;</span>from the Heard Island outbreak was worse than originally feared, with <b>76% mortality</b> among Elephant Seal pups.</p><p>Meanwhile,<b> <a href="https://www.agriculture.gov.au/campaigns/birdflu/latest-data#introduction_data">Australia's bird flu count </a></b>continues to rise, with the latest figure showing more than 700 confirmed events, and in excess of 63,000 hotline reports by the public.&nbsp;</p><p></p><div class="separator" style="clear: both;
